core.definition: A person who often complains, especially about small or unimportant things.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PLAY, and the final -er is an r-colored schwa, so pronounce the r lightly. Do not say 'kum-PLAY-nah,' which sounds British or non-rhotic.

nuance.connotation: Negative. Calling someone a complainer is an insult, so avoid saying it directly to a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use complainer for someone who grumbles all the time, often at work or on a team. It is informal and mildly insulting, so do not call someone that to their face. Softer ways to describe the person are 'He always has something to say about it' or 'She's not shy about voicing concerns.'

distinctions.note: A critic offers reasoned evaluation and often suggestions, while a complainer grumbles without offering solutions.
Whiner is more childish and refers to a whiny tone, while complainer is broader and can describe adults.
Grumbler suggests quiet, muttered discontent, while complainer suggests open and repeated complaints.

examples.everyday: Don't mind Ray; he's a complainer, but he's harmless.
examples.professional: Some team members are chronic complainers, but their feedback about the build times has been useful.
examples.analytical: A complainer's voice is easy to dismiss, yet the pattern of complaints often reveals structural failures.

nuance.analogy: A habitual complainer is like a smoke alarm that goes off over every piece of toast: people start tuning it out, even when there is a real fire.
nuance.etymology: From complain plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Using complainer as a polite way to describe someone with a concern; it is insulting.
Saying complainant when you mean a habitual grumbler.
Dropping the r in casual speech, saying 'kum-PLAY-nuh.'

senses.definition: Free; provided at no charge.
senses.example: complimentary drinks

senses.definition: In the nature of a compliment.
senses.example: a complimentary remark

senses.definition: With respect to the closing of a letter, formal and professional.
senses.example: He ended the cover letter with a complimentary close, Respectfully yours.

core.definition: Free of charge, offered as a gift by a business, or expressing praise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEN, the third syllable. In fast speech the middle t often sounds like a soft d, so it's MEN-duh-ree with a flapped t. The final -ary is pronounced 'ree', not 'air-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; a complimentary item is welcome, and a complimentary remark is kind.
nuance.usage_note: In American restaurants, hotels, and shops, complimentary means free, as in 'complimentary bread' or 'complimentary breakfast'. A server might say 'this dessert is on the house' as a more casual phrase. The sense of praise is less common in speech; say 'nice compliment' instead. Don't confuse it with complementary, which means things that go well together.

distinctions.note: Complementary means things that go well together or complete each other; complimentary means free or praising.
Free is the everyday word; complimentary sounds more polished and is typical in service settings.

examples.everyday: The hotel gave us a complimentary breakfast, so we only paid for coffee on the side.
examples.professional: Clients get a complimentary onboarding session, so schedule it before the invoice goes out.
examples.analytical: A complimentary review can praise a work so generously that it hides the flaws a reader most needs to see.

nuance.analogy: Like a free sample at a store: you didn't pay for it, and the shop is showing off what it has.
nuance.etymology: From compliment, from French compliment, with the suffix -ary.
common_mistakes: Confusing complimentary with complementary, which is a different word.
Using complimentary only for praise; in everyday American speech it usually means free of charge.
Stressing the first syllable, as in KAHM-plih-men-tair-ee; the main stress is on MEN.

conversation.text: The chips and salsa are complimentary.
They brought us a complimentary dessert for our anniversary.
The hotel has a complimentary breakfast.
My boss was really complimentary about the dinner I planned.

senses.definition: The tendency of a statistical model to become less and less accurate over time in real-world conditions.
senses.example: After the pandemic, our fraud model's accuracy dropped because of concept drift in customer behavior.

core.definition: In machine learning, the gradual change over time in the relationship between a model's inputs and the outcome it predicts, which lowers its accuracy.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on DRIFT, while concept keeps a lighter first syllable, KAHN-sept, with a short final t. Non-native speakers often stress both words equally or drop the t at the end of concept.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical, but it signals a problem: teams use it when a model is quietly getting worse.
nuance.usage_note: Data scientists and machine learning engineers use concept drift constantly in meetings, dashboards, and design reviews. Americans also use the verb form, saying a model is drifting, which means its performance is slipping. Outside technical work the phrase sounds jargony, but it's fine to use it with coworkers. Don't confuse it with data drift, which refers to changes in the inputs alone.

distinctions.note: Data drift means the distribution of inputs has changed, while concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the target has changed, so the same inputs now mean something different.
Model decay is a general term for any loss of accuracy over time, while concept drift names one specific cause of it.

collocations: retrain the model to handle concept drift

examples.everyday: Our spam filter keeps missing scams lately, which is probably concept drift because the spammers changed their tricks.
examples.professional: The fraud model's precision fell about 15 percent over two quarters, so we're adding concept drift alerts to the monitoring dashboard.
examples.analytical: Concept drift undermines the assumption that past data represents future conditions, so a model that performed well at deployment cannot be trusted indefinitely.

nuance.analogy: Like a city map drawn twenty years ago: the streets are still there, but the neighborhoods have changed, so the map leads you wrong.
nuance.etymology: Concept from Latin conceptus 'something conceived'; drift from Middle English drift, from Old Norse drift 'a driving'.
common_mistakes: Treating concept drift as a verb phrase, as in 'the model concept drifts' instead of 'the model is experiencing concept drift'
Confusing it with data drift, which describes input changes rather than changes in the relationship

concept-drift.etymology: Concept refers to the hidden relationship between the inputs and outputs of the model.

conversation.text: Concept drift means the relationship between inputs and the target changes over time.
Fraud models suffer from concept drift because fraudsters adapt their tactics.
We retrain monthly and monitor for concept drift with a rolling accuracy check.

senses.definition: The act of condemning or pronouncing to be wrong.
senses.example: Her public condemnation of the report surprised colleagues who had praised its methods.

senses.definition: The act of judicially condemning, or adjudging guilty, unfit for use, or forfeited; the act of dooming to punishment or forfeiture.
senses.example: The court's condemnation of the unsafe apartment building forced residents to relocate within thirty days.

senses.definition: The state of being condemned.
The ground or reason of condemning.
senses.example: Repeated safety violations were the stated condemnation for the old bridge.

senses.definition: The process by which a public entity exercises its powers of eminent domain.
senses.example: The city began condemnation proceedings to acquire the farmland needed for the new highway.

core.definition: A strong statement that something is wrong, or an official judgment that someone is guilty or deserves punishment.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on NAY, the second-to-last syllable, and the first syllable is a secondary stress. The middle vowels are reduced to a quick uh, so do not pronounce every letter fully.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It signals serious disapproval or a severe legal or moral judgment, so it is strong for everyday disagreement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use condemnation for serious matters such as wrongdoing, unsafe buildings, or public moral judgments in news and religious contexts. In ordinary conversation people say criticism or disapproval instead, because condemnation sounds dramatic. A natural reply to a condemnation of a public figure is often a question such as 'Do you think the condemnation was fair?'

distinctions.note: Criticism can be mild and constructive, while condemnation is a stronger, more final judgment of wrongdoing.
Disapproval is a feeling or attitude, whereas condemnation is a public or formal statement of blame.

examples.everyday: My neighbor got a lot of condemnation online after she parked in the fire lane.
examples.professional: The company issued a public condemnation of the harassment and fired the manager involved.
examples.analytical: Her condemnation of the policy rests on the claim that it punishes the innocent without due process.

nuance.analogy: Like a judge's gavel coming down, condemnation is a final verdict rather than a passing comment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin condemnare, to condemn, from com- (intensive) and damnare, to damn.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as KAHN-duh-muhn-ay-shun; the main stress is on NAY.
Using condemnation for mild disagreement, which sounds far too harsh in everyday talk.
Saying 'make a condemnation'; the usual phrase is 'issue a condemnation' or 'express condemnation'.

senses.definition: That is able to be condensed; that can undergo condensation.
senses.example: Water vapor is condensable, so it forms droplets on the cold glass.

core.definition: Able to be changed from a gas or vapor into a liquid, or made denser and more compact.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DEN, and the last two syllables are weak: suh-bul. Do not pronounce the final -able as 'ABE-ul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical description.
nuance.usage_note: Condensable is used mainly in chemistry, physics and engineering. Both condensable and condensible appear in American references, with condensible common in technical writing; check which one your journal or company uses. In everyday talk Americans say that steam condenses into water rather than using this adjective.

distinctions.note: Condensed is the ordinary adjective for something already made denser or shorter, like condensed milk; condensable describes what can be condensed.
Volatile means evaporates easily; condensable describes the reverse change, from vapor into liquid.
Compressible means can be squeezed into less volume; condensable refers to a change of state, though the two overlap in gases.

examples.everyday: Steam from the shower is condensable, so the mirror fogs up when the vapor hits the cold glass.
examples.professional: The lab report lists the condensable fraction of the emissions, which we measure separately from the gas phase.
examples.analytical: A substance is condensable only under specific temperature and pressure conditions, so its classification depends on the environment as much as its chemistry.

nuance.etymology: From Latin condensare 'to make dense', from con- 'together' and densus 'thick', with the suffix -able.
common_mistakes: Using condensable as a verb; the verb is condense, and the adjective describes a substance.
Assuming one spelling is always correct; both condensable and condensible appear, so follow the style of your field.

senses.definition: In a confidential manner.
Spoken of in a private manner.
senses.example: She told me confidentially that the layoffs would be announced before the end of the month.

core.definition: In a private way, telling something only to a trusted person so others will not know.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on DEN, the third syllable. The '-tial' ending is pronounced 'shuh', and the last syllable is 'lee', not 'lee-uh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals trust and discretion, though it can sound conspiratorial if used with exaggeration.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use 'confidentially' with phrases like 'Confidentially, I think...' or 'Between us...' to introduce private information. In business it appears in workplace communication, such as 'Please handle this confidentially.' A natural reply is 'Of course, I won't tell anyone,' or 'Don't worry, it stays between us.'

distinctions.note: 'Privately' means away from others in general, while 'confidentially' specifically involves secret information shared in trust.
'Secretly' often implies hiding something on purpose from someone, while 'confidentially' implies a trusted sharing of information.
'Off the record' is a more journalistic or informal phrase meaning not for publication, while 'confidentially' is used in everyday and workplace speech.

examples.everyday: Confidentially, Tom told me he's thinking about quitting, so don't mention it to anyone.
examples.professional: Please send the salary data to me confidentially, and don't forward it to anyone outside HR.
examples.analytical: The surveyor recorded responses confidentially, so no individual answer could be traced back to the participant.

nuance.analogy: Like a sealed envelope passed from one trusted hand to another.
nuance.etymology: From 'confidential' (from Latin confidere, 'to trust fully') plus the English suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'confidently', which means with self-assurance.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'con-fi-DEN-shal-ly' with an extra syllable.

senses.definition: An official indicator that things will happen as planned.
senses.example: We will send you a written confirmation of your hotel booking.

senses.definition: A verification that something is true or has happened.
senses.example: The announcement in the newspaper was a confirmation of my suspicions.

senses.definition: A ceremony of sealing and conscious acknowledgement of the faith in many Christian churches, typically around the ages of 14 to 18; considered a sacrament in some churches, including Catholicism, but not in most Protestant churches.
senses.example: On Sunday, the sixteen-year-olds prepared for confirmation at St. Mark's church.

senses.definition: An act whereby something conditional or voidable is made sure and unavoidable, especially the possession of an estate.
senses.example: The court's confirmation of the estate made the transfer legally final and irrevocable.

core.definition: Proof or notice that something is true or settled; also a Christian rite in which baptized persons affirm their faith.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress is on 'MAY', with secondary stress on 'kahn'. The middle 'fer' reduces to 'fur', and the ending is 'shun', not 'tion' as spelled.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; reassuring when it settles doubt. In religion it is solemn and positive.
nuance.usage_note: In daily American life, 'confirmation' is the email or number proving a booking, order, or appointment ('Do you have a confirmation number?'). In science and logic it means evidence that supports a hypothesis. In churches, it names the rite of confirming baptismal faith, usually in the teen years.

distinctions.note: Verification is the process of checking something; confirmation is the result or notice that it is correct.
Proof is conclusive; confirmation may merely strengthen a belief or claim.
Corroboration is independent evidence supporting a claim, often in legal or investigative settings.

examples.everyday: I never got a confirmation email for the hotel, so I'm going to call them.
examples.professional: We need written confirmation from the client before we deploy the model to production.
examples.analytical: A single confirmation does not prove a theory, and Popper argued that scientists should seek falsification instead.

nuance.analogy: Confirmation is the nod that tells you your guess was right.
nuance.etymology: From Latin confirmatio, from confirmare, 'to strengthen' (com- + firmus, 'firm').
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable: 'CON-firmation'.
Pronouncing the ending as 'tee-on' instead of 'shun'.
Calling a booking confirmation a 'confirm' (noun).

traditions.view: Confirmation is one of the seven sacraments of initiation. The bishop, or a priest with permission, anoints with chrism and the baptized receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit.
Chrismation is administered immediately after baptism, even to infants, by a priest anointing with holy chrism. It is the seal of the gift of the Holy Spirit and precedes first Communion.

Lutherans, Anglicans, and Presbyterians practice confirmation as a rite in which baptized youth publicly affirm their faith, but it is not a sacrament. Baptists and Pentecostals generally do not practice it, emphasizing believer's baptism.

confirmation.etymology: From Middle English *confirmacioun*, from Old French *confirmacion*, from Latin *cōnfirmātiō*, noun of process from *cōnfirmātus* (“confirmed”), perfect passive participle of *confirmo*, from *con-* (“with”) + *firmo* (“to firm or strengthen”).

senses.definition: To perplex or puzzle.
To stun or amaze.
senses.example: Her calm answer to the sudden question completely confounded the nervous interviewers.

senses.definition: To fail to see the difference; to mix up; to confuse right and wrong.
senses.example: Some people confound right and wrong when a cause seems noble enough.

senses.definition: To make something worse.
senses.example: Don't confound the situation by yelling.

senses.definition: To combine in a confused fashion; to mingle so as to make the parts indistinguishable.
senses.example: The renovations confounded the old and new wings into one indistinguishable structure.

senses.definition: To cause to be ashamed; to abash.
senses.example: His actions confounded the skeptics.

senses.definition: To defeat, to frustrate, to thwart.
senses.example: Sudden storms repeatedly confounded our plans to hike the ridge before sunset.

senses.definition: (dated) To damn (a mild oath).
senses.example: Confound you!
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: A confounding variable.
senses.example: We controlled for age as a confound, since older respondents were more likely to own cars.

core.definition: To confuse or puzzle someone so that they cannot easily understand a situation or decide what to do.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, FOWND, with the diphthong ow as in cow. The first syllable is a weak schwa, so do not stress the first syllable as KON-found.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It suggests frustration or being thrown off, and it often appears in phrases like confound expectations, which sound more neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use confound mostly in formal writing and in phrases like 'confound expectations' or 'confound the experts'. In everyday speech people say 'confuse' or 'throw me off'. The adjective 'confounded' is sometimes used as a mild, old-fashioned exclamation of frustration.

distinctions.note: Confuse is the everyday word for making someone unsure; confound is more formal and can add a sense of surprise or frustration.
To puzzle means to be hard to solve or explain, while confound adds a stronger sense of baffling or defeating someone's understanding.
Confound can mean to mix up two things, as in confounding one idea with another, which is a more formal version of mix up.

examples.everyday: The plot twist totally confounded me; I had no idea who did it.
examples.professional: The new vendor's pricing model confounds our forecasts, so we need to revisit the assumptions.
examples.analytical: Historians often confound correlation with causation when they rely on only one source.

nuance.analogy: Like a tangled fishing line that keeps the reel from turning, so you cannot make progress.
nuance.etymology: From Old French confondre, from Latin confundere, 'to pour together, mix up'.
common_mistakes: Using confound as a simple synonym for every kind of confusion, when confuse is more natural in everyday speech.
Stressing the first syllable as KON-found.

senses.definition: To stand or meet facing, especially in competition, hostility or defiance; to come face to face with.
senses.example: It is important that police officers learn to deescalate situations in which someone confronts them aggressively.

senses.definition: To deal with.
senses.example: confront a problem

senses.definition: To bring someone face to face with something.
senses.example: We should confront him about the missing money.

senses.definition: To come up against; to encounter.
senses.example: Inter Milan are to confront Juventus in the final.

senses.definition: To engage in confrontation.
senses.example: Rather than avoid the issue, she chose to confront her manager about the unfair schedule.

senses.definition: To set a thing side by side with; to compare.
senses.example: Before publishing, we confronted the revised estimates with last year's audited figures.

senses.definition: To put a thing facing to; to set in contrast to.
senses.example: The sermon confronted the pride of the powerful with the humility of the poor widow.

core.definition: To face a problem, person or difficult situation directly, often to deal with it or challenge it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FRUNT, and make the r clearly in American English. Do not add an extra syllable or a long vowel; the final t is crisp and unreleased before the end of the word.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somewhat negative. It suggests a direct, sometimes tense or confrontational encounter, so context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'confront' for facing an unpleasant issue or person, as in 'I confronted my roommate about the dishes.' It can sound intense, so for milder situations, 'talk to' or 'bring up' is more natural. In formal writing, it is common for challenges and problems.

distinctions.note: 'Face' is milder and more general, often used for accepting a situation, while 'confront' implies direct opposition or a need to deal with something hostile or difficult.
'Challenge' focuses on disputing a claim or position, whereas 'confront' stresses the direct, physical or emotional encounter with a problem or person.

examples.everyday: I finally confronted my neighbor about his dog barking all night, and he was pretty apologetic about it.
examples.professional: We need to confront the data quality issue head-on in the next sprint instead of hoping the pipeline fixes itself.
examples.analytical: Any serious theology must confront the problem of evil without reducing it to a simple puzzle that we can solve by definition.

nuance.analogy: To confront a problem is like stepping up to a closed door instead of walking around it: you face the thing directly and deal with it.
nuance.etymology: From French confronter, from Late Latin confrontare, 'to face, to bring face to face', from Latin con- 'together' and frons 'forehead, front'.
common_mistakes: Adding a preposition, as in 'confront with the problem'; the standard pattern is 'confront a problem' or 'confront someone about something'.
Using 'confront' for mild disagreements, which can sound more aggressive than the speaker intends.
Stressing the first syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural to American ears.

confront.etymology: From Middle French *confronter*, borrowed from Medieval Latin *confronto*, from *con-* + *frons* (“front, forehead”).

senses.definition: Giving consent; agreeing to something.
senses.example: The law prohibits payment for sex, even between consenting adults.

senses.definition: Done with the consent of all parties involved.
senses.example: consenting sex

core.definition: Giving permission or agreeing to something, such as a proposal, an action, or a request from someone else.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SENT. The noun consent is stressed on the first syllable (KON-sent), but the verb and adjective move the stress to the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In most settings it sounds clear and respectful, but in phrases like consenting adults it carries serious legal and ethical weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use consenting most often in legal, medical, and ethical contexts, and in the phrase consenting adults. In everyday speech people more often say okay with it, fine with it, or I'm on board. A natural reply to a request is to say yes, I'm consenting, or simply to agree.

distinctions.note: Agreeing is about holding the same opinion; consenting is about giving permission for an action someone proposes.
Consensual describes an agreement that is mutual and freely given; consenting describes one person giving permission.
Willing describes wanting to do something; consenting describes allowing it, even if you do not especially want to.

examples.everyday: Are you consenting to the photo, or should I delete it?
examples.professional: The vendor is consenting to a thirty-day extension if we sign the revised contract by Friday.
examples.analytical: Under contract doctrine, a consenting party is bound only by the terms it has knowingly accepted.

nuance.analogy: A consenting person is like a gatekeeper who chooses to open the gate and let the action through.
nuance.etymology: From Latin consentire, 'to agree, to feel together,' from con- 'together' and sentire 'to feel.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in the noun consent (KON-sent), when the adjective is stressed on the second syllable.
Using consenting to mean simply agreeing with an opinion, when it usually means permitting an action.

senses.definition: Having the quality of preserving from loss, decay, or injury.
senses.example: The sealed jars have a conservatory quality that keeps the fruit from spoiling all winter.

senses.definition: (rare) Relating to conservation.
senses.example: The commission reviewed the conservatory measures proposed for the wetlands along the river.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: A music school.
A drama school. (Can we verify this sense?)
(historical) A school or clinic for orphans.
senses.example: In the 1800s, the conservatory took in abandoned children and taught them useful trades.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (rare) A storehouse, a repository.
senses.example: The old library served as a conservatory of rare manuscripts for the entire region.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (uncommon) A greenhouse, a glass-walled building for cultivating delicate plants.
senses.example: Every winter we visit the botanical conservatory to see the orchids and tropical palms.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: A glass-walled room attached to a house, used for plants or relaxing, or a school for advanced study of music or drama.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SUR, and the last two syllables are -tor-ee with a clear American r. The middle vowels are quick and reduced, so do not give each syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The house-room sense sounds pleasant and domestic, while the music-school sense sounds prestigious and serious.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use conservatory for a music school, such as the Peabody Conservatory in Baltimore, or for a glassed sunroom attached to a house. The drama-school sense is mainly British; in the US, people say drama school or a theater program. In casual talk, many Americans just say sunroom or greenhouse.

distinctions.note: A greenhouse is built mainly for growing plants; a conservatory is usually an attached, decorative room used for living space as well.
A sunroom is the everyday American term for a glassed room in a house; conservatory is a more formal or British-sounding word for the same thing.

examples.everyday: We ate breakfast in the conservatory because the morning light there is so nice.
examples.professional: Our music department's partnership with the local conservatory gives students performance credit for the spring recital series.
examples.analytical: As an institution, the conservatory preserves musical traditions by training each generation in disciplined performance.

nuance.analogy: A conservatory is like a greenhouse for talent: glass walls, controlled conditions, and carefully tended growth.
nuance.etymology: From Latin conservatorium, 'place for preserving', via Italian conservatorio, which originally meant an institution for orphans.
common_mistakes: Using conservatory for an ordinary greenhouse where plants are grown for sale.
Putting the stress on the -VA- syllable, as in kun-ser-VAY-tor-ee.
Using the British drama-school sense in American contexts without explaining it.

senses.definition: Having been carefully thought out; maturely reflected upon.
senses.example: It is my considered opinion that the accused is innocent.

core.definition: Carefully thought out, deliberate and reasoned rather than hasty.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SID; the -ered ending is a weak, reduced syllable, and the final d is a clear sound. Do not add an extra syllable like 'kun-SID-er-ed'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it signals wisdom and careful judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use considered most often in phrases like 'a considered opinion,' 'a considered response,' or 'after considered thought.' It sounds deliberate and somewhat formal, so it suits business letters, reviews, legal statements and serious discussions. In casual talk, people say 'well thought out' or 'careful.' A considered reply is not simply a long one; it is reasoned and balanced.

distinctions.note: Deliberate can mean intentional, even negative (a deliberate insult); considered means carefully reasoned.
Thoughtful can mean kind or reflective; considered describes an answer or judgment that has been carefully worked out.
Careful describes a process or manner; considered describes the result or judgment.

examples.everyday: I'd like a considered answer from you, not just the first thing that pops into your head.
examples.professional: The team wants a considered recommendation on the vendor before Friday's review.
examples.analytical: Her considered judgment, reached after years of study, departs sharply from the prevailing consensus.

nuance.analogy: A considered decision is like a recipe tested and adjusted before serving, not a dish thrown together in a rush.
nuance.etymology: From consider, from Latin considerare 'to examine closely'; the adjective developed from the past participle.
common_mistakes: Using considered to mean considerate; a considerate person is kind to others, while a considered answer is carefully reasoned.
Pronouncing it with an extra syllable, as 'kun-SID-er-ed'.

senses.definition: Deserving contempt.

core.definition: Deserving strong disrespect; so bad, cruel, or dishonest that people look down on it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on TEMP. The final -ible is a reduced syllable, so say it as buhl, not as a separate long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative; calling something contemptible is a harsh moral judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contemptible in serious criticism of behavior, such as lying, cruelty, or betrayal. It is stronger than bad or unfair and can sound very harsh in casual talk. In everyday conversation, people often say that is despicable or that is low instead.

distinctions.note: Despicable is similar in strength and common in speech; contemptible is slightly more formal and emphasizes that the thing deserves scorn.
Contemptible describes the thing deserving contempt; contemptuous describes the person who shows contempt.

examples.everyday: Stealing money from your own grandmother is contemptible, and I don't care what your reason was.
examples.professional: Taking credit for a teammate's work in a status report is contemptible, and it should be addressed directly.
examples.analytical: Hobbes thought that betraying a trust is contemptible because it undermines the very basis of social life.

nuance.analogy: A contemptible act is like a pebble in a shoe: small in the eyes of some, but it makes everyone around it wince.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin contemptibilis, from Latin contemptus, past participle of contemnere, to despise.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as kon-TEMP-tuh-bul with the stress in the wrong place.
Using contemptible to mean looked down on in a neutral way; it implies a strong moral judgment.

senses.definition: Each of the traditional main regions into which the Earth’s land surface is divided, including both an extent of mainland and various conventionally associated islands, etc; namely, Africa, Europe, Asia, Australasia/Oceania, North America, South America, and Antarctica.
senses.example: Antarctica is the only continent without a permanent human population.

senses.definition: A large connected expanse of something in general.
senses.example: The forest seemed like a continent of green stretching to the horizon.

senses.definition: One of the main contiguous landmasses, separated by water or geological features, on the surface of a planet, sometimes including its continental shelves and the islands on them.
senses.example: Geologists believe that the continents drifted apart over hundreds of millions of years.

senses.definition: Exercising self-restraint; controlled, temperate with respect to one’s bodily needs or passions, especially sex.
senses.example: She remained continent throughout her years of ministry, and her discipline inspired others.

senses.definition: Having voluntary control over one’s urination or defecation.
senses.example: After the surgery, my grandmother was continent again within a few weeks.

core.definition: One of the seven large landmasses of the Earth, such as Africa, Asia, Europe, or North America, usually defined by convention as well as geology.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, KAHN, and the middle syllables are quick, unstressed vowels. Say KAHN-tih-nunt, not kun-TIN-ent as in continental.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain geographic term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use continent in everyday talk, school, news, and travel, usually with 'the' before the name, as in the African continent. The adjective continent, meaning self-controlled, is formal and mainly medical or literary, and in ordinary talk people say 'able to control' or 'dry' for bladder control. Americans also say 'continent' for Europe in casual talk about travel, but usually name the specific country.

distinctions.note: A country is a nation with its own government, and several countries can share one continent.
An island is surrounded by water and is smaller; a continent is a huge landmass, although Australia is sometimes called both.
A subcontinent is a large region within a continent, such as the Indian subcontinent, and is less formally defined.

examples.everyday: My cousin just took a new job on a different continent, so we only talk on video now.
examples.professional: Our European and Asian teams share one dashboard, but each continent has its own reporting deadline.
examples.analytical: The boundary between continent and island is partly a matter of convention rather than a sharp natural fact.

nuance.analogy: Like a very large island that is too big to call an island, a continent is defined by convention as much as by geology.
nuance.etymology: From Latin terra continens, 'continuous land', from continere, 'to hold together'.
common_mistakes: Confusing continent with country, saying Africa is a country instead of a continent.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables with a long ee sound, as in kun-TIN-ent, instead of KAHN-tih-nunt.

continent.etymology: Borrowed from Latin *continens*, noun use of present participle of *contineo* (“to contain”).

senses.definition: Synonym of European.
Pertaining to the colonies of British North America covered by the Continental Congress.
senses.example: Continental currency lost much of its value during the war, frustrating ordinary families in Massachusetts.

senses.definition: Synonym of European (a denizen of Europe)
senses.example: Our tour guide joked that the Continentals always arrive at dinner an hour late.

senses.definition: A denizen of the colonies of British North America covered by the Continental Congress.
senses.example: Among the colonists, every Continental in Philadelphia debated independence through that long summer.

core.definition: Relating to the mainland of Europe, as opposed to Britain or Ireland, or to the 48 contiguous states of the United States.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on NEN, and the first syllable has a lighter stress. End with a reduced vowel and l, so say -tul, not -tahl or -tent.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the word is a plain descriptive term in set phrases.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use continental mainly in set phrases: continental breakfast, a light hotel meal of pastries, toast, coffee, and juice; continental U.S., meaning the 48 states; and continental Europe, meaning mainland Europe, not Britain. As a noun, continental for a European person is dated or informal, so people normally say European.

distinctions.note: European describes people, things, or the whole continent; continental is narrower and often means mainland Europe as opposed to Britain or Ireland.
Intercontinental means between or across continents, as in an intercontinental flight; continental means relating to one continent or its mainland.

examples.everyday: The hotel just serves a continental breakfast, so I'll grab a muffin and some coffee.
examples.professional: Our Berlin office handles all of continental Europe, while London covers the UK.
examples.analytical: Calling a tradition continental philosophy says more about English-speaking institutions than about the geography of the thinkers themselves.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a region the mainland to set it apart from the islands around it.
nuance.etymology: From continent plus the adjective suffix -al, from Latin continens, 'continuous' land.
common_mistakes: Using continental for a British person; Americans would say British, not continental.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying KAHN-tuh-nen-tul or kahn-tuh-nen-TAHL, when the main stress is on NEN.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or involving a contribution.
senses.example: Our employer runs a contributory pension plan, so I pay a percentage of every paycheck.

senses.definition: Tending to contribute to a result.
senses.example: Poor sleep was a contributory factor in her declining focus at work.

senses.definition: A person or thing that contributes.
senses.example: The foundation listed every donor and contributory in its annual report.

core.definition: Helping to cause or bring about a result, often as one of several factors.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on TRIB, the second syllable, and the final syllable is a light, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a cause or factor without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contributory mostly in formal, legal, medical, and analytical writing, as in 'a contributory cause' or 'a contributory factor.' In casual talk they would say 'part of the reason' or 'one factor.' In legal contexts, 'contributory negligence' is a specific term for shared fault.

distinctions.note: Contributing is the common everyday adjective for something that helps; contributory is more formal and often used with factors or causes.
Contributive is rare and mostly literary; contributory is the standard word in American formal and technical writing.

examples.everyday: The heat was a contributory factor, so we had to stop the hike early.
examples.professional: The outage had several contributory causes, including a misconfigured server and a delayed patch.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that economic pressure was a contributory cause of the revolution, though not the only one.

nuance.analogy: Like one ingredient in a recipe that helps shape the final flavor without being the whole dish.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contributorius, from contribuere, to bring together.
common_mistakes: Using contributory as a noun in place of contributor; the noun form means a person or thing that contributes.
Confusing it with contributing in casual speech, where contributing is more natural.

contributory.etymology: From earlier *contributary*, from Middle English *contributarie*, from *con-* + *tributarie* after.

senses.definition: Easy in conversation, chatty.
senses.example: My uncle is quiet at work but surprisingly conversational over a cup of coffee.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or in the style of a conversation; informal and chatty.
Involving a two-way exchange of messages, such as between a client and a server.
senses.example: We switched the service to a conversational protocol so the client and server can exchange several messages per request.

senses.definition: Capable of engaging in conversation.
senses.example: The patient is awake and conversational.

core.definition: Informal and relaxed, like ordinary talk; relating to the style or tone of everyday conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SAY, and the -tion ending is pronounced shun. The final -al is a light syllable that sounds like nul.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests friendliness, ease, and approachability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often describe a tone or style as conversational, as in 'a conversational tone' for a blog post or speech. In technology, 'conversational AI' refers to chatbots and voice assistants. For basic speaking ability, people say 'conversational Spanish,' meaning enough to chat but not to read or write formally.

distinctions.note: Colloquial describes specific words or expressions used in casual speech, while conversational describes the overall tone or style of talk.
Chatty describes a person who talks a lot and enjoys chatting, while conversational describes a relaxed style that anyone can use.

examples.everyday: His tone was so conversational that I forgot we were in a job interview.
examples.professional: The chatbot uses a conversational style that customers find easy to follow.
examples.analytical: Plato's dialogues adopt a conversational form that draws readers into the search for truth.

nuance.analogy: Like talking over coffee with a friend instead of giving a lecture from a podium.
nuance.etymology: From conversation, with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Saying 'conversation English' instead of 'conversational English.'
Using it as a noun for a talk; conversation is the noun.

senses.definition: An uncontrolled fit, as of laughter; a paroxysm.
senses.example: We fell into convulsions of laughter when the substitute teacher mispronounced his own name.

senses.definition: Violent turmoil.
senses.example: Earthquakes and convulsions of nature shake Earth on a regular basis.

senses.definition: Hysteric in nature.
An intense, paroxysmal, involuntary muscular contraction.
senses.example: The drug triggered convulsions that shook his whole body, and he had to be rushed to the ER.

core.definition: A sudden, violent upheaval or disruption, often a dramatic shake-up in a society, economy or natural system.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VUL. The first vowel and the -ion ending are both reduced, and -sion is pronounced 'shun', not 'zhun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests violent disruption, pain or loss of control, though it can be used for laughter in a playful way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use convulsion mostly for physical fits or large political, economic or social upheavals. For laughter, people more often say 'doubled over' or 'in stitches,' though 'convulsed with laughter' is used in writing. A natural phrase in conversation is 'The whole office went into convulsions when the boss tripped.'

distinctions.note: Seizure is the medical term for a sudden episode in the brain, while convulsion usually describes the violent shaking or spasm of the body.
Upheaval means a major change or disruption, while convulsion adds a sense of violent shaking or spasm.

examples.everyday: The whole table went into convulsions of laughter when Dad tried to sing the national anthem.
examples.professional: The merger caused convulsions across the sales team for months, with people changing roles every few weeks.
examples.analytical: Historians describe the revolution as a convulsion that dismantled centuries of feudal order in a few years.

nuance.analogy: A convulsion is like an earthquake: a sudden shake that breaks apart what seemed stable.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convulsio, from convellere, to pluck or tear away.
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing the ending as 'zhun'; the American pronunciation is 'shun'.
Confusing convulsion with conversion or conclusion, which look similar but have different meanings.
nuance.biblical_note: In Mark 9:20 the RSV describes a boy thrown into convulsions by a spirit, and in Luke 9:39 the spirit convulses him until he foams. The Greek word behind these passages is sparassō, meaning to tear or throw into violent spasm. In both passages Jesus heals the boy, showing his authority over the spirit.

senses.definition: Prepared by cooking.
Corrupted by conversion through a text format, requiring uncooking to be properly listenable.
Partially or wholly fabricated, falsified.
Done in, exhausted, pooped.
In trouble; in a hopeless situation.
Hungover.
Brain-damaged from drug use.
senses.example: Don't bother talking to that guy—he's cooked from all the coke he used to do.

core.definition: Prepared by heating, so that the food is ready to eat and no longer raw.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable. The -ed after a voiceless k is pronounced as t, so say kookt, not kook-ed or kookd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for food. Informally, 'I'm cooked' is negative, meaning exhausted or in serious trouble.
nuance.usage_note: Cooked is the ordinary word for food prepared by heat, as in 'Is the chicken fully cooked?' Informally, Americans say 'I'm cooked' to mean they are exhausted, or that they are in deep trouble after a mistake. In tech and data settings, 'cooked' can describe results that were manipulated, so be careful with it when discussing numbers.

distinctions.note: Done means cooked to the desired level, while cooked simply means heated and prepared.
Raw is the opposite: not heated. Cooked means heated enough to eat safely or to taste good.

examples.everyday: Is the chicken fully cooked? I don't want anyone getting sick.
examples.professional: The dashboard shows data from a preprocessing step, so we should audit the pipeline before presenting the numbers.
examples.analytical: If the researchers' results were cooked in advance, the study tells us more about their goals than about the world.

nuance.analogy: Like bread that has risen and set in the oven, cooked food has changed from raw to ready.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of cook.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing -ed as a separate syllable; cooked has only one syllable.
Using 'I'm cooked' in formal writing, where it sounds too casual.

cooked.etymology: From the past tense of the verb *cook*.

senses.definition: The outer surface of a piece of flint.
senses.example: The flint's cortex was pale and chalky, so the knapper cracked the stone open carefully.

senses.definition: The outer layer of an internal organ or body structure, such as the kidney or the brain.
senses.example: Neurologists mapped activity in the visual cortex while volunteers looked at moving patterns on screens.

senses.definition: The tissue of a stem or root that lies inward from the epidermis, but exterior to the vascular tissue.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the root's cortex appeared as a broad band between the epidermis and the vascular tissue.

core.definition: The outer layer of an organ, especially the thin gray outer layer of the brain where thinking and sensory processing occur.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, KOR-. The r is strongly pronounced, and the final -tex sounds like 'teks,' not 'tecks' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise anatomical or biological term with no emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say cortex mainly in science and medicine, such as 'the visual cortex' or 'the prefrontal cortex.' In everyday speech people usually say 'the brain' or refer to a specific area by its common name. The plural is cortices, pronounced KOR-tuh-seez, or sometimes cortexes in casual writing.

distinctions.note: Brain refers to the whole organ; cortex refers only to its outer layer, which is the part most involved in higher thought.
Medulla is the inner part of an organ, while cortex is the outer layer, as in the kidney or brain.
Cerebrum is the large upper part of the brain, which contains the cortex; cortex is a layer within it.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the scan shows the outer layer of my brain, the cortex, looks normal.
examples.professional: The lab's neural model was trained to match activity patterns in the visual cortex.
examples.analytical: Philosophers of mind often ask whether the cortex alone can explain consciousness, or whether the whole nervous system must be included.

nuance.analogy: The cortex is like the bark of a tree: the outer layer that protects and surrounds the inner tissue where most of the work happens.
nuance.etymology: From Latin cortex, 'bark, rind, shell.'
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the plural incorrectly; use cortices, not cortexes, in technical writing.
Using cortex to mean the whole brain.
Stressing the second syllable, as kor-TEKS, instead of KOR-teks.

senses.definition: To incur a charge of; to require payment of a (specified) price.
senses.example: This shirt cost $50, while this was cheaper at only $30.

senses.definition: To cause something to be lost; to cause the expenditure or relinquishment of.
senses.example: Trying to rescue the man from the burning building cost them their lives.

senses.definition: To require to be borne or suffered; to cause.
senses.example: Ignoring the warning signs could cost the company millions in lost customer trust.

senses.definition: To cost (a person) a great deal of money or suffering.
senses.example: I can give you the names, but it'll cost you.

senses.definition: To calculate or estimate costs (such as expenses, or a price).
senses.example: I costed the repair work at a few thousand.

senses.definition: Amount of money (or time, etc.) that is required or used.
senses.example: The total cost of the new complex was an estimated $1.5 million.

senses.definition: A negative consequence or loss that occurs or is required to occur.
senses.example: Spending all your time working may earn you a lot of money at the cost of your health.

senses.definition: Quality; condition; property; value; worth; a wont or habit; disposition; nature; kind; characteristic.
senses.example: Nobody questioned the honest cost of the old farmer's character.

senses.definition: A cottise.
senses.example: The coat of arms displayed a narrow cost running diagonally beneath the lion.

core.definition: To require a certain amount of money, time, or effort to be paid, spent, or given up in order to obtain something.

pronunciation.tip: It is a one-syllable word, so the vowel is short and the final t is a clean stop. Do not add an extra vowel between the s and the t, as in 'kos-it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It shifts toward negative when it refers to a loss, harm, or sacrifice rather than a price.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cost constantly in shopping and everyday talk, as in 'How much does it cost?' The past tense and past participle are also cost, so 'It cost me twenty dollars' is correct. In business, 'costed' is used as a verb meaning to estimate the cost of something, but it is not used in everyday talk.

distinctions.note: Price is what the seller asks; cost is what something requires to obtain, which can include time, effort, or loss.
A charge is a specific fee applied to a service or purchase; cost is the total amount needed or spent.
Pay is the act of handing over money; cost describes how much it takes to get something.

examples.everyday: How much does a haircut cost at that place on Main Street?
examples.professional: The new vendor contract will cost us about fifteen thousand dollars a year, not including support.
examples.analytical: Every policy choice costs something, and an honest argument must name the trade-offs instead of hiding them.

nuance.analogy: Cost is like the bill that arrives at the end of a meal: it shows what you have to give up to get what you enjoyed.
nuance.etymology: From Old French coster, from Latin constare 'to stand firm, be fixed at a price'.
common_mistakes: Using 'costed' as the simple past of cost, which is wrong in everyday speech; the past is 'cost'.
Saying 'it costs for me' instead of 'it costs me' when the cost falls on a person.
nuance.biblical_note: In Luke 14:28, Jesus asks who does not 'count the cost' before building a tower, using the Greek word dapanē, meaning expense or outlay. The point is that discipleship requires weighing what it will demand. Isaiah 55:1 invites people to buy wine and milk 'without money and without price,' showing God's free gift.

senses.definition: A person who spends a lot of time sitting or lying down, often watching television, eating snacks or drinking alcohol.
senses.example: Being a couch potato won't let you help achieve your goals.

core.definition: An informal name for a person who spends much time sitting or lying on a couch, usually watching television and not exercising.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'couch' and on 'TAY' in 'potato', with 'pə' reduced to a quick schwa. The 't' in 'potato' is a flap, so it sounds like 'puh-TAY-duh-' in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'couch potato' jokingly or with mild criticism for someone who is lazy or inactive, often about watching TV or streaming shows. It is casual and common in everyday talk. Saying it about a friend can be teasing, but calling a person a couch potato directly may sound rude if they are sensitive about their health.

distinctions.note: Lazy is a general word for not wanting to work or act, while couch potato specifically refers to someone who spends time sitting and watching television.
A homebody likes staying at home but may be active; a couch potato is specifically inactive and passive.

examples.everyday: My brother says he's a couch potato on weekends, but he still runs five miles on Monday.
examples.professional: I'm trying not to be a couch potato during the holiday break, so I'm planning to go hiking with the team.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'couch potato' reveals a cultural anxiety about leisure, equating sedentary television watching with a moral and physical decline.

nuance.analogy: A couch potato is like a potato that has rolled onto the couch and stayed there, slowly sinking into the cushions.
nuance.etymology: Coined in American English in the late 20th century, combining 'couch' and 'potato' in a playful way.
common_mistakes: Saying 'couch potatoes' for a single person; the idiom is singular when describing one person.
Pronouncing 'couch' as 'coach'; the vowel is a diphthong like 'cow'.

couch-potato.etymology: coined by Tom Iacino in 1976 as a pun on boob tuber (from *boob tube* (“television”) and *tuber* (“potato”)); trademarked by Robert Armstrong from 1976–91.

conversation.text: I was a total couch potato all weekend, just watching TV.
My dog has turned into a couch potato in his old age.
Get off the couch, you couch potato. Let's go for a walk!

senses.definition: Asking for an extra item; "Could we get…" is the polite form.

core.definition: A polite request asking a server or host to bring extra paper napkins for your table.

pronunciation.respelling: kood wee get sum mor NAP-kinz
pronunciation.tip: The stress is on NAP in napkins, and the p is often lightly released before the z. Some speakers drop the p in casual speech, so you may hear 'NAP-kinz'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; asking for extras is routine and not considered demanding.
nuance.usage_note: This is a natural, everyday request at restaurants, cafes, and at home when guests need more. Americans typically say 'Could we get...' rather than 'Can I have...' in a restaurant. A friendly reply is 'Of course!' or 'Absolutely, I'll bring some right over.'

distinctions.vs: Could we get some more napkins? vs. Can we get more napkins?
distinctions.note: Could is slightly more polite and tentative, which is the usual tone when addressing restaurant staff.
Serviette is mainly British; Americans say napkin.

examples.everyday: Could we get some more napkins? The kids spilled everything.
examples.professional: Could we get some more napkins for the conference room, since the breakfast catering ran out?
examples.analytical: The request for more napkins reflects a small but telling gap between what a meal provides and what diners actually need.

nuance.analogy: Like asking for a spare roll of paper towels when the first one runs out.
nuance.etymology: Napkin comes from Middle English, from Old French nappe, a cloth, with the diminutive ending -kin.
common_mistakes: Using 'some more' with countable napkins without the plural: say 'napkins', not 'napkin'.
Saying 'Give me more napkins' sounds abrupt in a restaurant.

conversation.text: Sorry, the kids spilled. Could we get some more napkins?
These ribs are messy. Could we get some more napkins, please?
When you get a chance, could we get some more napkins?

senses.definition: Asks someone to say something again.

core.definition: A polite request asking someone to say something again because you did not hear or understand it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PEET in repeat, and the r is clearly rhotic. Could you reduces to 'kood yoo', and the final t of that is often dropped in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and polite; it is the standard way to ask for repetition and sounds helpful rather than rude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this on phone calls, in meetings, and when someone speaks quickly or quietly. It is more polite than 'What?' or 'Huh?', which can sound impatient. A common reply is 'Sure, I said the deadline is Friday.'

distinctions.vs: could you repeat that vs. what?
distinctions.note: What is blunt and can sound rude; could you repeat that is polite and standard.

distinctions.vs: could you repeat that vs. could you say that again
distinctions.note: Both are polite; say that again is slightly more casual and often used when you want the exact words.

examples.everyday: Sorry, the music was loud. Could you repeat that?
examples.professional: Could you repeat that last point about the budget? I didn't catch the number.
examples.analytical: Could you repeat that premise? I want to test whether the argument holds if we define the term differently.

nuance.analogy: Like rewinding a recording to hear a sentence you missed.
nuance.etymology: Repeat comes from Latin repetere, to seek again or go over again.
common_mistakes: Dropping could and saying 'You repeat that' in a way that sounds like an order.
Stressing repeat on the first syllable (REE-peat) instead of rih-PEET.

conversation.text: Sorry, could you repeat that? I missed the last part.
Could you repeat that account number, please?
"Could you repeat that?" "Sure, the meeting is at 3:30."

senses.definition: That counteracts.
senses.example: The counteractive measures, such as extra sleep and lower caffeine, eased his anxiety quickly.

core.definition: Tending to reduce, offset, or neutralize the effects of something else.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on KOWN, and the final -ive is a short, reduced 'iv'. The middle -ter- is a quick, r-colored syllable that learners often overpronounce as 'tar'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a helpful effect that offsets a problem, as in medicine, engineering, or policy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use counteractive mostly in technical, medical, or formal writing. In everyday speech they say 'offsetting' or 'it helps balance it out.' Do not confuse it with counterproductive, which means something backfires; a counteractive measure works as intended.

distinctions.note: Counterproductive means an action backfires and makes the goal worse; counteractive means it reduces an unwanted effect.
Preventive stops a problem before it starts; counteractive works against a problem or effect that is already present.

examples.everyday: Opening the window has a counteractive effect on the stuffy air after cooking.
examples.professional: We added a counteractive check to offset the bias the model picked up from the older data.
examples.analytical: A counteractive force inside the system keeps the feedback loop from spiraling out of control.

nuance.analogy: A counteractive force is like a shock absorber, softening the bump before it reaches the seat.
nuance.etymology: From counteract plus -ive; counter- means against and act comes from Latin actus 'a doing'.
common_mistakes: Using counteractive when you mean counterproductive, which means backfiring.
Pronouncing the middle syllable as 'tar' in KOWN-tar-AK-tiv; the vowel is a reduced schwa.

senses.definition: A person who delivers messages.
A company that delivers messages.
A company that transports goods.
senses.example: We hired a courier company to deliver the contracts to the Chicago office.

senses.definition: A user who earns access to a topsite by uploading warez.
senses.example: Within a year, he had uploaded enough files to become a courier on the private topsite.

senses.definition: A person who looks after and guides tourists.
senses.example: Our courier led the group through the old town, pointing out the cathedral and markets.

senses.definition: To deliver by courier.
senses.example: We'll have the contract couriered to you.

core.definition: A person or company that carries packages, documents, or messages quickly from one place to another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The 'ou' sound is short, like 'book', and the final syllable is a weak American 'er', not 'ear'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a service or person, so it carries no strong feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use courier for delivery people who carry documents, packages, or medical samples, often on a fast schedule. You may hear it for a bike messenger in a city or for a company like FedEx or UPS in business talk. In casual speech people often say 'delivery driver' or 'messenger' instead.

distinctions.note: A messenger usually carries a message in person, often on foot or by bike, while a courier usually handles packages or time-sensitive documents for a business.
A delivery driver is a general term for anyone who brings goods, while a courier implies a more specialized or fast service.

examples.everyday: The store said the new couch would come by courier on Thursday, so someone needs to be home.
examples.professional: We should use a courier for the signed contracts, since the client needs them by tomorrow morning.
examples.analytical: The courier in the old epistolary culture bore the weight of trust, since the message was only as reliable as the person who carried it.

nuance.analogy: A courier is like a relay runner who carries the baton from one station to the next, and the race depends on speed and reliability.
nuance.etymology: From Old French courier, from Italian corriere, from correre, to run, from Latin currere.
common_mistakes: Confusing courier with currier, a person who dresses leather.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'koo-REE-er'.

courier.etymology: From a convergence of Middle English *corour*, *currour*, from Old French *coreor*, agent noun of *corir* (“to run”), and Middle English *courier*, a borrowing of Middle French *courrier*, from Italian *corriere*.

senses.definition: A legal case to be resolved in a court.

core.definition: A legal dispute brought before a court, where a judge or jury decides the outcome.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on case, with court slightly weaker. Pronounce the r in court clearly, and don't let the t blur into the k of case.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a legal matter without judging who is right.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use court case for any matter a judge hears, civil or criminal, and in legal conversation often say simply 'a case'. In everyday talk, 'lawsuit' usually means one private party suing another, and 'trial' means the hearing itself. Saying 'I have a court case next month' to a coworker is natural.

distinctions.note: A lawsuit is a civil action brought by one party against another, usually for money; a court case can also be criminal.
A trial is the hearing stage of a court case where evidence is presented; a court case covers the whole matter from filing to appeal.

examples.everyday: My cousin's court case over the car accident finally ends next month.
examples.professional: Legal says the court case over the vendor contract is set for March, so we should hold the data until then.
examples.analytical: The court case turned less on the facts than on whether the statute even applied to digital records.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee's final review, a court case is the formal stage where a dispute is settled by someone with authority.
nuance.etymology: Court from Old French cort, from Latin cohors 'enclosed yard'; case from Latin casus 'a falling, chance'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the court case' for the building; the building is the courthouse.
Pronouncing court with the vowel of 'cart' instead of the vowel of 'door'.

senses.definition: Somebody with whom one works.
senses.example: He heard from a coworker that the company planned to merge those departments.

senses.definition: A person in the lowest common denominator, especially regarding popular culture.
senses.example: This is the most coworker movie I've ever seen.

core.definition: A person who works for the same employer or on the same job as you, often in the same office or team.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the 'work' syllable, not the 'co' syllable. The final 'er' is reduced and r-colored, so it sounds like 'ker.'

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It is a friendly, everyday word for people you work with, and it usually sounds warm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'coworker' in everyday conversation about jobs, lunch, or office life. It is usually written as one word, though 'co-worker' also appears in older style guides. In formal writing, 'colleague' is sometimes used, especially for professionals in academic or business settings.

distinctions.note: Colleague is more formal and often used for professionals in fields like law, medicine, or academia, while coworker is the everyday word for anyone you work with.
Teammate means a member of your specific team, while coworker refers more broadly to anyone at the same company.
A boss has authority over you, while a coworker is a peer with no such authority.

examples.everyday: My coworker recommended a great taco place near the office.
examples.professional: I'll loop in my coworker from the data team so she can review the model.
examples.analytical: The coworker relationship, unlike friendship, is structured by shared tasks rather than chosen affinity.

nuance.analogy: A coworker is like a fellow rower in a boat: you may not have chosen each other, but you have to pull in the same direction.
nuance.etymology: From co- meaning together, plus worker.
common_mistakes: Stressing the 'co' syllable, pronouncing it 'KOH-wur-ker,' instead of stressing 'work.'
Using 'coworker' for a boss or manager, when the word refers to peers only.

conversation.text: A few coworkers and I go to lunch every Friday.
My coworker covered for me while I was at the doctor's.
She's not just a coworker; she's become a really good friend.

senses.definition: Abruptly stern measures or disciplinary action; increased enforcement.
senses.example: The city announced a crackdown on illegal parking downtown after complaints from merchants.

core.definition: A sudden, strict effort by authorities to stop or punish a specific illegal or unwanted behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, crack, and the two words are joined into one, so down is reduced but not silent. The vowel in down is the ow sound of 'town'.

nuance.connotation: Negative for those affected, neutral from the authorities' view. It suggests harsh enforcement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crackdown mostly in news and everyday talk about police, schools, or companies, as in 'a crackdown on drunk driving.' The noun is one word, and the verb is the phrasal verb crack down. Because it suggests strict action, it can sound harsh when applied to people. Natural replies include 'Really? When did it start?' or 'Will it affect everyone?'

distinctions.note: Clampdown is nearly identical and common in news; it often implies tighter, more lasting control.
A sweep is a broad search or raid of an area; crackdown focuses on strict enforcement of rules or laws.
Reform means a change to improve a system; crackdown means strict enforcement, not necessarily improvement.

examples.everyday: The city announced a crackdown on people parking in the bike lanes.
examples.professional: Finance announced a crackdown on expense reports, so every receipt over fifty dollars now needs approval.
examples.analytical: A crackdown can reduce a visible problem in the short term, but critics ask whether it addresses the causes beneath the behavior.

nuance.analogy: A crackdown is like a sudden hard rain on a dry street: the change is fast and strong, but it may not last.
nuance.etymology: From the phrasal verb crack down, meaning to come down hard on something.
common_mistakes: Writing crack down as a noun in formal text; the noun is one word, crackdown.
Using crackdown of instead of crackdown on when naming the target of enforcement.

senses.definition: A female artisan.
senses.example: The craftswoman spent weeks hand-weaving the wool blanket for her daughter's wedding.

core.definition: A woman who is highly skilled at making things by hand or at a trade.

pronunciation.tip: Stress CRAFTS strongly and give woman a weaker secondary stress. The vowel in 'woman' is the short 'oo' of 'book', so it sounds like 'woom-un', not 'wo-man'.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful. It emphasizes a woman's skill, though some people now prefer the gender-neutral 'craftsperson'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'craftswoman' when they want to specify a woman's gender, often in museums, histories or descriptions of artisans. In workplace writing, many people prefer 'craftsperson' unless gender is relevant. Americans would not normally say 'craftswomen' without context, but the plural is regular.

distinctions.note: Craftsperson is gender-neutral and the usual choice in modern workplace writing; craftswoman specifies a woman.
Artisan stresses traditional or artistic production and does not mark gender.
Craftsman is traditionally used for men and can sound dated when applied to women.

examples.everyday: My aunt is a craftswoman who restores antique furniture in her garage.
examples.professional: The museum hired a craftswoman to reproduce the damaged tapestry using period techniques.
examples.analytical: The exhibit reframes early American history by centering the work of women who were craftswomen, not merely household helpers.

nuance.analogy: A craftswoman is like a weaver at a loom: each thread is placed deliberately, and the pattern shows the skill of the hands.
nuance.etymology: Craft from Old English cræft; woman from Old English wīfmann, meaning a wife or female person.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'craftswoman' with the plural 'craftswomen' used incorrectly in singular contexts.
Pronouncing 'woman' as 'WO-man' with a long vowel, instead of the short 'oo' sound.

senses.definition: A line or mark made by folding or doubling any pliable substance; hence, a similar mark, however produced.
senses.example: His pants had a nice sharp crease.

senses.definition: The circle around the goal, which no offensive players may enter during play, unless after scoring.
senses.example: The goalie stayed inside the crease while the forward circled the net.

senses.definition: The area in front of each goal.
senses.example: The striker scrambled in the crease, desperately trying to poke the ball past the keeper.

senses.definition: A crack.
senses.example: A deep crease split the glacier ice, warning the hikers that the surface was unstable.

senses.definition: One of the white lines drawn on the pitch to show different areas of play; especially the popping crease, but also the bowling crease and the return crease.
senses.example: DRS showed he was out of the crease in a controversial run out review.

senses.definition: To make a crease in; to wrinkle.
senses.example: She creased the letter in half and slipped it into her coat pocket.

senses.definition: To undergo creasing; to form wrinkles.
senses.example: The linen shirt creases easily, so I iron it before every meeting.

senses.definition: To lightly bloody; to graze.
senses.example: The bullet just creased his shoulder.

core.definition: A line or mark made by folding, pressing or wrinkling paper, cloth or another flexible material.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long ee, and the r is rhotic before it. Do not say 'kriss' with a short i, which is a common mistake for learners.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a visible fold line, though it can be a sign of wear or carelessness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crease for folds in pants, shirts, paper and maps, as in 'iron out the creases.' In sports, crease means the marked area in front of a hockey or lacrosse goal. In cricket, the lines are called creases too, but Americans rarely talk about cricket.

distinctions.note: A wrinkle is usually a small, uneven line or fold, often from age or fabric; a crease is a sharper line created by folding or pressing.
A fold is the act or result of bending something over; a crease is the visible line the fold leaves behind.

examples.everyday: I hung my shirt in the closet, but there's still a crease down the sleeve.
examples.professional: The printed map had a crease across the middle, so we sent a fresh copy to the client.
examples.analytical: The crease in the manuscript becomes a metaphor for the text's division between public duty and private memory.

nuance.analogy: Like a fold left in a letter after it has been opened and closed many times.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English creste, a ridge or crest, related to crest.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'kriss' with a short i.
Using crease for a small skin wrinkle; use wrinkle or fine line for skin.

crease.etymology: From earlier English creast, from Middle English *crest* (“ridge, crest”).

senses.definition: Of or relating to Crete or its inhabitants.
An inhabitant or a resident of Crete.
senses.example: My colleague is a Cretan who grew up near Chania and still visits every summer.

core.definition: Of or relating to Crete, the Greek island in the eastern Mediterranean, or to its people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KREE. The t between a stressed and an unstressed vowel is often a quick flap that sounds like a soft d, and the ending is a reduced uhn.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing place, people, food or culture without emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Cretan for things from or belonging to the island, such as Cretan cheese or olive oil, and for its people. Crete itself is the name of the island, so Cretan is the adjective and the noun for an inhabitant. Use Greek when you mean the nation in general.

distinctions.note: Greek refers to Greece as a nation or its language and people generally, while Cretan specifies the island of Crete.
Minoan describes the Bronze Age civilization centered on Crete, not the modern people or things from the island.

examples.everyday: We had dinner at a little Cretan place near the marina, and the lamb was fantastic.
examples.professional: Our sourcing team is comparing Cretan olive oil producers for the new product line.
examples.analytical: Classical sources complicate Cretan identity, since the island's Greek and Minoan pasts overlap in complicated ways.

nuance.analogy: Like Sicilian to Sicily, the word ties a person or thing back to a specific island.
nuance.etymology: From Latin Creta, from Greek Krete, the name of the island.
common_mistakes: Saying KREH-tan with a short e and a hard stress on the second syllable
Using Cretan to mean all of Greece, when it refers only to the island
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible Cretans are the inhabitants of Crete, the Greek word being Krētes, meaning Cretans. Acts 2:11 lists Cretans among the visitors who heard the apostles speaking in their own languages at Pentecost in Jerusalem. Titus 1:5 says Paul left Titus on Crete to set right what was unfinished and to appoint elders in each town. Titus 1:12 reports a saying attributed to a Cretan prophet about the people's character, which Paul uses to explain the need for sound teaching.

senses.definition: The state of being crisp.
An instance of being crisp.
senses.example: The crispness of the autumn apples made them perfect for the pie.

core.definition: The quality of being firm, fresh, and brittle, as in food, or sharp, clean, and neat, as in air, paper, clothing, or style.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The sp is one tight cluster, and the -ness ending is a short, reduced syllable with no vowel inserted between p and n.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests freshness, cleanliness, and precision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crispness for cool autumn air, fresh cotton sheets, a fresh apple, or a clean, precise style of writing. For fried or baked food, crispiness is more common. In everyday talk you might say 'I love the crispness in the air this morning,' and the word also works well in professional writing about design or style.

distinctions.note: Crispiness focuses on the texture of fried or baked food; crispness is broader and covers air, fabric, paper, and clear style.
Freshness describes newness or recent making; crispness describes a clean, firm, sharp quality.

examples.everyday: I love the crispness of the air this time of year, it makes walking the dog so nice.
examples.professional: The new design has a crispness that makes the dashboard easier to scan during a quick meeting.
examples.analytical: The essay's crispness comes from its refusal to hedge, so each claim lands with precision.

nuance.analogy: Like the snap of a fresh sheet being pulled tight, clean and sharp.
nuance.etymology: From crisp, from Old English crisp 'curled', plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Writing crispyness with an extra y; the noun is crispness or crispiness.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes it sound like a different word.

senses.definition: The external, hardened layer of certain foodstuffs, including most types of bread, fried meat, etc.
senses.example: The bread's golden crust was crunchy on the outside and soft inside.

senses.definition: The bread-like base of a pizza.
A slice of bread cut from the end of a loaf; the heel.
