distinctions.note: Quadruplicate means to make four copies; quadruple means to multiply by four in size, amount, or number.
Double means multiply by two; quadruple is two doublings, so the increase is much bigger.

examples.everyday: Rent in our neighborhood has nearly quadrupled in ten years, which is crazy.
examples.professional: Our cloud costs quadrupled after the migration, so we need to optimize the storage tiers this quarter.
examples.analytical: If the sample size quadruples, the standard error is roughly halved, which is why larger samples help so much.

nuance.analogy: Quadrupling is like doubling twice: you double a number, then double it again.
nuance.etymology: From Latin quadruplus, 'fourfold,' from quadri- 'four' and -plus, 'fold.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, KWAD-ruh-pul, instead of the second.
Using quadruple to mean just 'a lot more' when the increase is not exactly four times.

senses.definition: Argumentative; fond of or prone to quarreling.
senses.example: She's too quarrelsome to participate in a civil conversation.

core.definition: Tending to argue, or easily starting quarrels with others.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The final syllable is a weak 'sum' with a reduced vowel, not a full 'some' sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative, describing someone as difficult or combative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'quarrelsome' to describe a person who likes to argue, often in a critical way. It sounds somewhat formal or literary in everyday talk, so people more often say 'argumentative' or 'picks fights.' A natural description is 'He gets quarrelsome when he drinks.'

distinctions.note: Argumentative is the more common everyday word and describes someone who likes debate, while quarrelsome is stronger and suggests hostility.
Combative suggests readiness to fight, often physically or in a competition, while quarrelsome focuses on arguing.

examples.everyday: Don't invite Mark if you want a calm evening; he gets quarrelsome after a couple of drinks.
examples.professional: A quarrelsome team member can derail a project even when the technical work is excellent.
examples.analytical: Her analysis treats a quarrelsome disposition less as a personal flaw than as a symptom of unmet needs within the group.

nuance.analogy: Like a dry match that catches fire at the slightest spark: a quarrelsome person sparks conflict easily.
nuance.etymology: From 'quarrel' plus the suffix '-some,' meaning 'inclined to.'
common_mistakes: Using it for a single argument rather than a habit or personality trait.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'some.'

senses.definition: Of the nature of a quintessence (in all senses); being or relating to the ultimate essence of something.
senses.example: Her quintessential kindness shone through in every letter she wrote to her grandchildren.

senses.definition: The fundamental essence of something.
senses.example: For him, honesty was the quintessential of a good friendship.

core.definition: Being the perfect or most typical example of something; representing its essence in the purest form.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the third syllable, SEN, with a secondary stress on the first syllable. The 'ti' is a quick 'tih', and the ending is 'shul'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises something as perfectly typical or ideal for its type.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use quintessential often in reviews, travel writing, sports commentary and everyday praise, as in 'a quintessential New York diner.' It is more formal than 'classic' but still natural in conversation. Replies are usually simple agreement, such as 'Totally.'

distinctions.note: Typical means usual or ordinary; quintessential means the purest or most perfect example of its kind.
Classic can mean a well-known or excellent example; quintessential adds the idea that it captures the whole essence of the type.

examples.everyday: That little diner on the corner is the quintessential American breakfast spot, with pancakes and bad coffee.
examples.professional: This sprint is the quintessential example of how the team should handle a risky release without slowing down.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard treats despair as the quintessential expression of the self that refuses its own relation to God.

nuance.analogy: A quintessential example is like a stop sign in the middle of a road: it is so clearly what it is that nobody has to guess.
nuance.etymology: From quintessence, from Medieval Latin quinta essentia, 'fifth essence', with the adjective suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying kwin-tuh-SEN-shuhl with a flat 'tuh' instead of 'tih'.
Using quintessential for something merely typical; it is a strong word for the perfect example.

senses.definition: To make someone feel in a better mood.

core.definition: To make someone feel happier or more hopeful, especially after they have been sad or disappointed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SUM in someone's and on SPIR in spirits. In fast speech someone's sounds like sum-wunz, so do not pronounce every syllable separately.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes kindness, encouragement or comfort.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this in everyday talk, notes and at work when a friend, coworker or child is sad. Lift someone's spirits is equally common. It sounds warm and natural, not stiff. A good reply to thanks is 'Glad I could help.'

distinctions.note: Cheer up is a direct request or command to someone to feel better, while raise someone's spirits describes a general lift in mood caused by an action or event.
The two are almost identical in meaning, and both are common; lift sounds slightly lighter in everyday speech.

collocations: a card to raise her spirits

examples.everyday: Thanks for the flowers, they really raised my spirits after that rough week.
examples.professional: A short note from the CEO can raise the team's spirits after a hard product launch.
examples.analytical: Pastoral writers often argue that scripture can raise the spirits of the grieving, though it does not always explain their suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like opening a window in a stuffy room, it lets in fresh air and light.
nuance.etymology: Spirit comes from Latin spiritus, meaning breath.
common_mistakes: Using raise for a physical lift, as in raising a box; in this idiom it means boosting mood.
Writing 'raise the spirit' in the singular when speaking about a group; the plural spirits is normal.

senses.definition: One who ratifies.
senses.example: The governor was the final ratifier of the treaty, signing it after the legislature voted.

senses.definition: One who is in favor of ratification.
senses.example: As a strong ratifier, she spent months campaigning for the constitution's adoption across the state.

core.definition: A person or body that formally approves an agreement or decision, making it official.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is an unstressed r-colored schwa, and the middle syllable is a clear 'fye' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'ratifier' in speech. It is found in legal and political writing, where it refers to a person, legislature, or state that formally approves a treaty or amendment. In normal conversation people say 'the people who approved it' or 'the signing body'.

distinctions.note: A signatory signs an agreement, while a ratifier formally approves it, sometimes later and in a separate step.
Ratification is the act of approving, while a ratifier is the person or body that does it.

examples.professional: The board is the final ratifier of the budget, so please send the draft to them on Monday.
examples.analytical: Who counts as a legitimate ratifier of a constitution is a central question in political philosophy.

nuance.analogy: A ratifier is like the final judge who stamps a decision as official.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ratus, 'fixed, approved', plus facere, 'to make'.
common_mistakes: Using 'ratifier' for the person who signs a document; the signer is the signatory.
Pronouncing it as 'rat-IF-ier'; the stress is on the first syllable.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being rational; due exercise of reason; reasonableness.
senses.example: His sudden loss of rationality was brought on by excess drink.

senses.definition: Objective consideration.
senses.example: Such a discussion deserves rationality, not emotional gut reactions.

core.definition: The quality of thinking or acting in a logical, sensible way based on reasons and evidence.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the third syllable, NAL, and the final syllables are reduced, so say rash-uh-NAL-ih-tee. Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce the -ity ending as a full ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it praises sound judgment but can sound cold when used to describe someone's decision.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rationality mostly in academic, economic, philosophical, and formal business contexts, such as discussing rational choice theory. In everyday talk, people usually say that something makes sense or that a decision was reasonable. The word can sound stiff if you use it to describe a friend's ordinary choice.

distinctions.note: Reasonableness describes an acceptable or fair attitude, while rationality focuses on the logical process behind a judgment.
Logic is a formal system of valid inference; rationality is the broader quality of making decisions that fit one's reasons and goals.

examples.everyday: I respect her rationality, even when I disagree with her choice to buy a used car.
examples.professional: The model assumes buyers act with full rationality, which doesn't match what we see in our customer survey data.
examples.analytical: Kant locates the rationality of moral action in the will's capacity to act on universal principles.

nuance.analogy: Rationality is like a good referee who makes calls based on the rules and the play, not on who is winning.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rationalis, from ratio, reason.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in RASH-ih-nal-i-tee.
Using rationality for a single sensible decision; it refers to the general quality of reasoning.

rationality.etymology: From *rational* + *ity*, from French *rationalité*, from Late Latin *rationalitas* (“rationality, reasonableness”), from Latin *rationalis* (“reasonable”).

senses.definition: To extend beyond (something).
Synonym of get past.

core.definition: To stretch your hand or arm beyond or around something to get what is behind it or past it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the particle 'past' more than 'reach.' Make the vowel in 'past' short and open, and do not confuse it with 'pass.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, used for physical actions in everyday situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say reach behind, reach over or reach around for most physical situations, and reach past is a bit less common. You might say it when describing a gap or a narrow space, such as reaching past a bottle to get the milk. It is informal and used in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: Reach over implies extending across the top of something; reach past suggests going beyond it or around it to get to something.
Pass means move by or go through; reach past is specifically about extending your arm beyond an obstacle.

examples.everyday: I had to reach past the jars in the back of the fridge to find the butter.
examples.professional: The technician had to reach past the server rack to access the cable.
examples.analytical: The poem's speaker reaches past the visible world toward something the senses cannot grasp.

nuance.analogy: Like sliding your hand past the cans on a shelf to find the one at the back.
nuance.etymology: Reach from Old English raecan, combined with past, from the Middle English passen, meaning to go beyond.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'past' with 'pass' in speech.
Using 'reach past' for arriving at a place; use 'get past' or 'pass' for that.

senses.definition: To activate again.

core.definition: To make something that was inactive or turned off start working or be used again.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, 'AK.' The prefix re- is 'ree,' not 'ray,' and the final 'ate' is a clear 'ayt.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and practical, used for accounts, services, memberships and systems.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reactivate for accounts, licenses, subscriptions and memberships, as in 'I need to reactivate my card.' For computers or systems that have been turned off, they often say restart or reboot. In spoken English, bring back or turn back on is common too.

distinctions.note: Reboot means restart a computer or device; reactivate means bring back an account, service or feature that was inactive.
Restore usually means returning something to an earlier state; reactivate means making something active again.

examples.everyday: I need to reactivate my gym membership, since I stopped going back in March.
examples.professional: Could you reactivate my account so I can access the shared drive this morning?
examples.analytical: Some dormant genes can be reactivated by changes in the chemical environment of the cell.

nuance.analogy: Like turning a power switch back on in a house that has been closed for the winter.
nuance.etymology: From re- (again) plus activate, from Latin activus, meaning acting or doing.
common_mistakes: Putting the main stress on the first syllable, as in 'REE-ack-tivate.'
Using reactivate for restarting a computer; reboot or restart is more natural there.

senses.definition: A person who reads.
senses.example: an early reader, a talented reader

senses.definition: A person who reads a publication.
senses.example: 10,000 weekly readers

senses.definition: A person who recites literary works, usually to an audience.
senses.example: The famous reader drew a packed crowd to the library for her dramatic poetry evening.

senses.definition: A proofreader.
senses.example: The reader caught three misspelled names in the galley before the book went to print.

senses.definition: A person employed by a publisher to read works submitted for publication and determine their merits.
senses.example: The publisher's reader recommended rejecting the manuscript after reading only the first chapter.

senses.definition: A position attached to aristocracy, or to the wealthy, with the task of reading aloud, often in a foreign language.
senses.example: The duke hired a reader to read French novels aloud to his wife every evening after dinner.

senses.definition: Any device that reads something.
senses.example: a card reader, a microfilm reader

senses.definition: A book of exercises to accompany a textbook.
senses.example: Students should complete the exercises in the reader before starting the next chapter of the textbook.

senses.definition: An elementary textbook for those learning to read, in a native language or a foreign language.
senses.example: Appletons’ School Readers

senses.definition: A literary anthology.
senses.example: Her literature course assigned a reader containing short stories from six different centuries.

senses.definition: A lay or minor cleric who reads lessons in a church service.
senses.example: The old man served as reader at the parish, reading the lessons each Sunday morning.

senses.definition: A newspaper advertisement designed to look like a news article rather than a commercial solicitation.
senses.example: The article about the new spa was actually a reader paid for by the spa company.

senses.definition: Reading glasses.
senses.example: Grandpa couldn't read the menu without his reader, so he pulled them from his pocket.

senses.definition: Marked playing cards used by cheaters.
senses.example: The dealer slipped a reader into the deck, so the gambler knew every high card.

senses.definition: At Eton College, a lesson for which pupils are sent back to their separate school houses.
senses.example: At Eton, the boys were sent back to their houses for a reader that afternoon.

core.definition: A person who reads books, texts or other written material, often for pleasure or study.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so say REE-der, not REE-dair.

nuance.connotation: Positive; calling someone a reader usually suggests they read a lot.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reader for anyone who reads, from a casual book lover to a professional proofreader. In newspapers and websites, 'readers' means the audience, as in 'letters from readers'. To describe someone who reads a lot, say 'I'm a big reader' or 'She's an avid reader'.

distinctions.note: An e-reader is a device for reading digital books; a reader is a person who reads.
Audience refers to listeners or viewers as well as readers; reader is specific to written material.
A scholar is a specialist who studies a field in depth; a reader may simply enjoy reading.

examples.everyday: My sister is an avid reader, and she finishes a novel almost every week.
examples.professional: Our technical reviewers are careful readers, so write each section for someone who reads closely.
examples.analytical: The careful reader notices that the author's second chapter quietly contradicts the first.

nuance.analogy: Like a radio receiver: it takes in signals and turns them into meaning.
nuance.etymology: From read, from Old English rǣdan, plus the suffix -er meaning one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -er as 'air'; in American English it is an r-colored 'uh'.
Using reader for a university rank; in British universities 'reader' is an academic title, but Americans say 'associate professor'.

reader.etymology: From Middle English *reder*, *redar*, *redere*, *redare*, from Old English *rēdere*, *rǣdere* (“a reader; scholar; diviner”), from **rādāri*, equivalent to *read* + *-er*.

senses.definition: (dated) The genuine thing, neither a substitute nor an imitation.
senses.example: Those are the real McCoy, not knockoffs, my grandfather's original 1950s records.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Something that is genuine and authentic, not a copy, substitute, or fake. Used mainly in the phrase 'the real McCoy'.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KOY, and the first word is stressed lightly, so 'real' is not a long vowel like 'reel' in 'reel in a fish'. Link the words smoothly, and keep the 'm' of 'McCoy' weak and quick.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises authenticity and quality, often after a doubt about whether something is a copy.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in casual speech to confirm that something is authentic, such as food, music or a sports performance. It is somewhat dated, but everyone understands it and it still appears in everyday talk and movies. A natural reply is 'Yeah, it's the real McCoy' or simply 'Definitely, that's the real thing'.

distinctions.note: Nearly identical in meaning; 'the real McCoy' is more colloquial and has a folksy, slightly old-fashioned flavor.
'Genuine' is neutral and works in any context, including formal writing, while 'the real McCoy' is informal and conversational.

collocations: a bit of the real McCoy

examples.everyday: Is this barbecue sauce homemade? It's the real McCoy, my neighbor's family recipe.
examples.professional: The vendor's demo looked polished, but when we ran the real McCoy on production data, the latency doubled.
examples.analytical: Critics debate whether the film is the real McCoy of the noir genre or merely a stylish imitation of its conventions.

nuance.analogy: Like a cup of coffee brewed from actual beans versus instant powder that only looks similar in the jar.
nuance.etymology: The origin is disputed; popular stories link it to boxer Norman 'Kid' McCoy or rum-runner Bill McCoy, but neither is proven.
common_mistakes: Pluralizing the phrase as 'real McCoys' when the idiom is used in the singular.
Using it in formal writing, where 'genuine' or 'authentic' is more appropriate.

real-mccoy.etymology: Corruption of Scots *real MacKay*, this latter attested in 1856 as “A drappie o’ the real MacKay”.

senses.definition: Synonym of backup camera.
senses.example: The rearview camera showed a child standing behind the car, so I stopped before reversing.

core.definition: A camera mounted on a vehicle that shows the area behind it on a screen, to help the driver when reversing.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound, the main stress falls on REAR, the first word, not on -VIEW. The second word camera is stressed on KAM and ends in a weak ruh sound, not 'cam-EER-a'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, descriptive term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'backup camera' in everyday talk, especially when asking a friend or a car salesperson about a feature. 'Rearview camera' is common in car manuals, dealership listings, and safety reports. Don't confuse it with the 'rearview mirror,' which is the glass mirror on the windshield.

distinctions.note: The two terms are synonyms, but 'backup camera' is more common in everyday American speech.
A rearview mirror is a reflective glass mirror that needs no electronics, while a rearview camera is an electronic camera with a display screen.

examples.everyday: Turn on the rearview camera before you back out of the driveway, because the kids' bikes are back there.
examples.professional: All new fleet vans now come with a rearview camera as standard equipment, which cut our parking-lot incident reports in half.
examples.analytical: The rearview camera shifts attention from the mirror to a screen that flattens distance, so drivers judge space differently.

nuance.analogy: It is like giving the car a pair of eyes in the back, with the view shown on a small screen on the dashboard.
nuance.etymology: Rearview combines rear (the back part) and view; camera comes from Latin camera, meaning chamber or vault.
common_mistakes: Confusing the camera with the rearview mirror, which is a different device.
Stressing the second word too strongly. The main stress is on REAR, and camera has a light secondary stress.

senses.definition: Pertaining to, or characterized by recapitulation.
senses.example: The professor's recapitulative summary at the end of each lecture helped students review the key ideas.

core.definition: Summarizing or restating the main points of something said or written, often at the end of a discussion, argument, or section.

pronunciation.tip: Primary stress falls on PICH, the third syllable, and the -tive ending is a short 'tiv', not 'teev'. Keep the middle syllables reduced to 'uh' and do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals structure and clarity in academic or formal writing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use recapitulative in conversation; it is an academic or formal adjective. In everyday speech they say 'summary,' 'recap,' or 'quick review.' In teaching and presentations, a recapitulative slide or section is the review at the end.

distinctions.note: Both mean summarizing; recapitulatory is rarer and more old-fashioned, so recapitulative is the safer choice in modern academic writing.
A summary is the everyday noun for a short restatement; recapitulative is an adjective describing a passage or statement that sums things up.

examples.professional: The meeting ended with a recapitulative slide listing each owner, deadline, and open risk.
examples.analytical: The essay's recapitulative conclusion restates the thesis without new evidence, which makes its structure clear but its argument static.

nuance.analogy: A recapitulative summary is like replaying the highlights of a game before the final score is announced.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin recapitulare, to sum up under headings, from re- (again) and capitulum (a heading or chapter).
common_mistakes: Confusing recapitulative (adjective) with recapitulation (noun); the adjective describes a passage, while the noun names the act.
Using it in casual speech, where 'summary' or 'recap' sounds more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: Recapitulation is a theological term, not a common biblical word, but Ephesians 1:10 is the key passage behind Irenaeus's teaching that Christ sums up all things in himself. The Greek verb anakephalaioo means to sum up or bring under one head. Ephesians 1:10 says God's plan is to unite all things in Christ, in heaven and on earth. Romans 13:9 describes the commandments as summed up in the command to love one's neighbor.

senses.definition: To match (something or someone which one currently perceives) to a memory of some previous encounter with the same person or thing.
senses.example: I recognized his face immediately, although his voice was different.

senses.definition: To acknowledge the existence or legality of; to treat as valid or worthy of consideration.
senses.example: The US and a number of EU countries are expected to recognize Kosovo on Monday.

senses.definition: To acknowledge or consider (as being a certain thing or having a certain quality or property).
senses.example: Slavery is widely recognized as immoral.

senses.definition: To realize or discover the nature of something; apprehend quality in.
senses.example: She could recognize the quiet strength in her new colleague within a week.

senses.definition: To show formal appreciation of, as with an award, commendation etc.
senses.example: His services were recognized in a testimonial.

senses.definition: To have the property to bind to specific antigens.
senses.example: The receptor is designed to recognize a specific viral protein on infected cells.

senses.definition: To cognize again.
senses.example: I think I recognize that voice from the conference call last spring.

core.definition: To identify someone or something you have seen, heard or known before.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced schwa. Pronounce the g clearly before n, so it is REK-uh-g-nize, not REK-uh-nize. Americans do not say the word with the stress on the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a mental act and carries no judgment, though 'recognize' someone's work is positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'recognize' constantly for identifying faces, voices and places, as in 'I recognize that song.' The verb can also mean officially acknowledging something, as in 'the company recognized the union' or 'they recognized my contribution.' The American spelling is recognize, not recognise.

distinctions.note: Realize means to become aware of something, often suddenly; recognize means to identify something already known.
Identify means to name or establish exactly what something is; recognize often relies on a feeling of familiarity.
Remember concerns stored memory; recognize concerns matching a present perception to a past one.

examples.everyday: Wait, I think I recognize that guy from the gym.
examples.professional: I recognize this pattern from last quarter, so let's check the data pipeline first.
examples.analytical: We recognize a person not merely by appearance but by the continuity of a life we have already encountered.

nuance.analogy: Recognizing is like matching a key to a lock you have opened before: the fit feels familiar at once.
nuance.etymology: From Latin recognoscere 'to know again', from re- 'again' and cognoscere 'to know'.
common_mistakes: Using 'recognize to' with a person when you mean 'recognize as' or 'recognize by'
Writing or saying recognise, which is British spelling and pronunciation patterns
Dropping the g in the pronunciation

recognize.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *reconoistre*, from Old French *reconoistre*, from Latin *recognosco*, first attested in the 16th century.

senses.definition: To begin again.

core.definition: To begin again after a pause or interruption.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the third syllable, mens, which rhymes with dense. The first syllable has secondary stress. Do not stress the first syllable, and do not pronounce the final s as z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it sounds polished and somewhat formal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'recommence' in everyday talk. They say 'start again,' 'pick up again,' or 'resume.' You may see it in formal reports, legal or diplomatic news, or in the formal speech of a presenter. Using it casually can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Resume means to continue what was interrupted and is far more common in American speech; recommence is more formal and emphasizes starting again.
Restart often refers to machines, computers or a process beginning from the start; recommence is more formal and used for activities like talks or work.

examples.everyday: Once the rain stops, we can recommence painting the fence.
examples.professional: Legal teams will recommence negotiations on the contract next Monday.
examples.analytical: Inquiry must recommence whenever a new premise is introduced, since no conclusion stands unchallenged.

nuance.analogy: To recommence is like restarting a song from the first line after the record has stopped.
nuance.etymology: From Old French recommencer, from re- 'again' and commencer 'to begin'.
common_mistakes: Using 'recommence' in casual speech where 'start again' or 'resume' is natural
Confusing it with 'recommend' because of the similar beginning

recommence.etymology: From Middle French *recommencer*, from Old French *recommencier*, equivalent to *re-* + *commence*.

senses.definition: In AI: A group that tests an AI system by trying to make it fail or misbehave.
senses.example: Before launch, the red team spent two weeks trying to trick the chatbot into giving dangerous advice.

senses.definition: An independent group employed to challenge an organization by assuming an adversarial role or point of view.
senses.example: The board hired a red team to challenge our five-year plan and find its weakest assumptions.

senses.definition: To challenge an organization by assuming an adversarial role.
senses.example: Before we commit, let's red team the proposal and see where it might break.

core.definition: A group that deliberately tries to find weaknesses in a system or plan by acting as an opponent, such as attacking a computer network or testing an AI model.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'team,' and 'red' is weakly stressed. Pronounce 'team' with a long 'ee' and a clear 't', and do not add an extra vowel between 'red' and 'team.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Red team is standard American jargon from military and cybersecurity circles, and it has spread into tech and business. A red team is typically set up by an organization to challenge its own plans, and the verb 'red team' is used in the same way. In casual speech the phrase is understood mainly by people who work in security, AI, or planning.

distinctions.note: A blue team defends a system; a red team attacks it to expose weaknesses.
A devil's advocate is one person arguing the opposing side; a red team is a formal group with a structured mandate.

examples.everyday: My sister works in cybersecurity, and her company has a red team that tries to break into their systems every month.
examples.professional: Before launch, we asked a red team to attack the authentication flow and report anything that could be exploited.
examples.analytical: A red team's value lies in its adversarial stance, which exposes assumptions that the planning group would otherwise leave unexamined.

nuance.analogy: A red team is like a sparring partner who uses real punches so you find your weaknesses before the real fight.
nuance.etymology: The color terms come from military war-gaming, where red stood for the opposing force and blue for one's own side.
common_mistakes: Saying 'red team' as a generic term for any opposition group outside security or AI.
Pronouncing 'red' with a long vowel, as in 'reed.'
Confusing red team with blue team, which defends rather than attacks.

red-team.etymology: Red was the color of the Soviet Union on maps during the Cold War, so "red team" represented the adversary during military simulations.

conversation.text: The red team found a way to extract the system prompt in under ten minutes.
Let's red-team the agent before it gets access to customer accounts.
In cybersecurity, a red team plays the attacker while the blue team defends.

senses.definition: Somewhat red.

core.definition: Somewhat red in color; having a red tint but not fully red.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on RED. The -ish ending is a short, weak syllable, so do not stretch it into a long ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It is used for hair, wood, skin, and other colors without strong feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reddish for hair, brown wood, sunsets, and autumn leaves, and it sounds natural in casual description. For hair, 'reddish-brown' or 'strawberry blonde' is also common. Use reddish for a loose, mild color, not for a bright, clear red.

distinctions.note: Red names the color clearly, while reddish suggests a softer or partial red.
Ruddy describes a healthy, flushed red skin tone, while reddish is a general color description.

examples.everyday: My daughter has reddish hair, just like her grandmother did when she was young.
examples.professional: The reddish warning light on the server rack means the cooling system needs attention.
examples.analytical: The painter's reddish undertones create a warmth that the cooler palette of the earlier series lacked.

nuance.analogy: Reddish is like a red crayon pressed lightly on paper: the red is there, but softened.
nuance.etymology: From red, with the suffix -ish, meaning somewhat or having the quality of.
common_mistakes: Writing reddish with a double d or missing the -ish ending.
Using reddish to mean bright red, when a clear, strong red is simply red.

senses.definition: Soiled with smoke or steam; smoky; foul.
Emitting a reek; smelly.
senses.example: The reeky gym socks under the bed made the whole bedroom smell awful.

core.definition: Smelling strongly of smoke, sweat or something foul; smoky or stinking.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -y is a long ee. It is easy to confuse with reedy, so listen for the k sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes something unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use reeky in everyday talk; they say smelly, stinky or smoky. You may meet it in older novels or in regional speech. For a strong smell in conversation, smelly is more natural.

distinctions.note: Smelly is the everyday word; reeky is more literary and suggests smoke or stale air.
Smoky describes the presence of smoke; reeky adds a foul, stale quality.

examples.professional: The old warehouse was reeky with diesel fumes, so we moved the meeting outside.
examples.analytical: The novel's reeky inn becomes a symbol of the decay that the family refuses to face.

nuance.analogy: Reeky is like a campfire smell that has soaked into your coat.
nuance.etymology: From reek, from Old English rēc, smoke or vapor.
common_mistakes: Confusing reeky with reedy; the spellings and meanings differ.
Using it in everyday speech where smelly would be more natural.

senses.definition: An additional helping of food or drink at reduced cost.
senses.example: Today it is $2 for a coffee, with free refills throughout the day.

senses.definition: That which serves to refill or replace something.
senses.example: Today it is $2 for a coffee, with free refills throughout the day.

senses.definition: Refueling, fuel to refill an empty fuel tank or other fuel container.
senses.example: Tank's empty. We need to go for a refill.

senses.definition: A product intended to replace the used contents of a container or the exhausted supply of a device.
senses.example: We're cutting back. No new printers or pens, just refills.

senses.definition: An act or process of refilling.
senses.example: capillary refill

senses.definition: A repeat of a prescription.
senses.example: I asked the pharmacist whether my blood pressure prescription still had a refill left.

senses.definition: To fill up once again.
senses.example: Can you refill my cup please? I've finished my coffee.

senses.definition: To repeat a prescription.
senses.example: My doctor agreed to refill my allergy medication without requiring another office visit.

core.definition: An extra serving of a drink or food, often at a reduced price, or a new supply of a medicine or product.

pronunciation.tip: The noun has its stress on the first syllable, REE. The verb is stressed on the second syllable, ree-FILL, so the stress shifts between noun and verb.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly, especially for drinks. For medicine, it is neutral and practical.
nuance.usage_note: In American restaurants, a free refill of coffee or soda is very common, and servers often ask 'Would you like a refill?' You can say 'Can I get a refill?' or 'Could I have a refill, please?' For prescriptions, Americans say 'Can I get a refill on my prescription?' and pharmacies say 'refills remaining'.

distinctions.note: Second helping means more food. Refill is common for drinks and for medicine, and it can also mean a new supply of a product.
Replenish is formal and used for supplies. Refill is everyday and used for containers, drinks and prescriptions.

collocations: get a refill on a prescription

examples.everyday: Could I get a refill on my iced tea, please?
examples.professional: Please submit the refill request for the printer cartridges before the end of the week.
examples.analytical: The refill of a glass is a small convention, but it reveals how restaurants trade generosity for repeat custom.

nuance.analogy: A refill is like filling a half-empty gas tank: the container is the same, but it is topped up to serve again.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English refillen, from re- and fill.
common_mistakes: Stressing the verb on the first syllable: the verb is ree-FILL, but the noun is REE-fill.
Asking for a refill of food, which sounds odd; say second helping or more instead.

conversation.text: Can I get a refill on my iced tea, please?
The server came by to refill our water glasses twice.
I need to stop by the pharmacy to get my refill.
I need a refill on my allergy medicine.
The pharmacy called; your refill is ready.

senses.definition: The act, or the result of refining; the removal of impurities, or a purified material.
senses.example: The refinement of crude oil removes sulfur and other impurities before it reaches gas stations.

senses.definition: High-class style; cultivation.
senses.example: The hotel's staff greeted guests with a refinement that felt rare in the city.

senses.definition: A fine or subtle distinction.
senses.example: The philosopher's argument depended on a refinement that most readers would miss.

senses.definition: A luxury.
senses.example: After years of camping, a hot shower felt like a refinement he could hardly afford.

senses.definition: Synonym of grooming (“review and prioritization process”).
senses.example: Our sprint planning includes a refinement session where the team reviews and prioritizes the backlog.

core.definition: Improvement by careful work, or a subtle detail that makes something better or more precise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, FINE. The final -ment is a light, reduced syllable, not a full vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies care, improvement or good taste.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use refinement for careful improvements to a product, model or plan, and for good manners or taste. In a workplace, 'a small refinement' is a helpful way to suggest a minor change. In casual talk, people more often say 'improvement' or 'tweak.'

distinctions.note: Improvement is general, while refinement suggests a careful, detailed adjustment to something that already works.
A tweak is a quick, informal change, while refinement is more deliberate and may take longer.

examples.everyday: The new coffee maker has a few small refinements that make it easier to clean.
examples.professional: The proposal needs a few refinements before we send it to the client on Monday.
examples.analytical: Each refinement of the definition narrows the claim, which shows how careful argument depends on distinction.

nuance.analogy: Refinement is like sanding a piece of wood: each pass removes rough spots until the surface is smooth.
nuance.etymology: From refine, with the suffix -ment, from Old French raffinement.
common_mistakes: Using refinement to mean refinery, which is a plant where oil or sugar is processed.
Stressing the first syllable, as in REE-fine-ment.

senses.definition: Any of several movements that promote reform.

core.definition: The belief in and promotion of gradual reform of a system or institution rather than revolutionary change.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FOR. The -ism ending is -iz-um with a reduced final vowel, not a full ism as in mist.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; supporters see it as careful progress, while radicals may criticize it as too slow.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reformism in political science, history and news analysis, often to describe a moderate approach. In conversation, people say they want incremental change or that they are moderate. Calling someone a reformist can signal to radicals that the person is too cautious.

distinctions.note: Reform is the change itself or the act of changing; reformism is the belief or movement that promotes such change.
Radicalism calls for fundamental change, often quickly; reformism prefers gradual, incremental change within the system.

examples.everyday: My neighbor doesn't want to tear down the school board; he just believes in reformism, fixing the budget one vote at a time.
examples.professional: The city council's reformism has produced steady improvements, but the budget problems will need a larger reorganization.
examples.analytical: Reformism assumes the system can be improved from within, a premise that radical critics often reject as naive.

nuance.analogy: Reformism is like renovating a house one room at a time while the family keeps living in it.
nuance.etymology: From reform plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using reformism to mean revolution; it means gradual change within a system.
Confusing reformism with reform: reform is the change, while reformism is the belief behind it.

senses.definition: Advocating reform of an institution or body.
Specifically, advocating reform and the gradual accumulation of small changes, as opposed to revolutionary action.
senses.example: The reformist senator favored gradual changes to the tax code rather than a complete overhaul.

senses.definition: One who advocates reform (of an institution).
senses.example: The hospital's new reformist wants to change how nurses are scheduled.

senses.definition: Specifically, one who advocates reform of society and the gradual accumulation of small changes, as opposed to revolutionary action.
senses.example: As a reformist, she believed patient, incremental change would do more than any revolution.

senses.definition: A member of a reformed religious denomination.
senses.example: Her great-grandparents were reformists who worshipped in a plain white church outside Grand Rapids.

senses.definition: (dated) An advocate of reform in the Church of England; a Reformer.
senses.example: In the sermon, the preacher praised the reformist who had challenged the bishops in 1560.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) An advocate or supporter of political reform in the United Kingdom. (Common from ca 1790 to 1830.)
senses.example: In 1825, the young reformist addressed a crowd in Manchester demanding a wider franchise.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Favoring gradual reform of an institution or system rather than revolutionary change.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FOR. The -ist ending is short, like mist, and should not be stretched into a long eest.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for moderates; it can sound like criticism from radicals or conservatives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reformist in political and academic writing about systems, such as a reformist candidate or a reformist wing. As a noun, it labels someone who seeks change step by step. In conversation, people more often say reform-minded or someone who wants to fix things. In church history, reformist can also mean a member of a reformed denomination, but that use is rare.

distinctions.note: Reformer is a general word for anyone who pushes for change; reformist often specifies that the change should be gradual and within the system.
Progressive is a broader political label with specific ideological meanings; reformist describes the method of change.

examples.everyday: My sister is a reformist, so she votes for candidates who want to fix the system without tearing it down.
examples.professional: The reformist approach here is to update the review process rather than replace the whole department.
examples.analytical: A reformist theology accepts the church's structure while calling for correction of its practices.

nuance.analogy: A reformist is like a gardener who prunes and feeds a tree instead of uprooting it.
nuance.etymology: From reform plus the suffix -ist, meaning one who supports or practices.
common_mistakes: Using reformist to mean revolutionary; it refers to gradual change.
Confusing reformist with reformer: a reformer may push for radical change, while a reformist usually favors gradual change.

senses.definition: Mode of rule or management.
senses.example: a prison regime

senses.definition: A form of government, or the government in power, particularly an authoritarian or totalitarian one.
senses.example: the dictator's regime

senses.definition: A period of rule.
A regulated system; a regimen.
senses.example: a fitness regime

senses.definition: A division of a Mafia crime family, led by a caporegime.
A set of characteristics.
senses.example: A typical annual water level regime would include a gradual summer drawdown beginning in early May.

core.definition: A government in power, especially an authoritarian one; also, a system or way of managing or controlling something.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, ZHEEM, and the first vowel is reduced to a quick 'uh'. The middle sound is the 'zh' of 'measure', and the ending is a long e, not a short i.

nuance.connotation: Often negative in political news, where the word suggests illegitimate or oppressive rule. In everyday talk about routines, such as a workout regime, it is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: In American news and political discussion, regime usually describes a government that is seen as authoritarian, and it carries criticism. For a legitimate elected government, Americans say government or administration. Outside politics, people say 'workout regime' or 'skincare regime' casually, but in health and medicine, regimen is the more precise and preferred word.

distinctions.note: Government is neutral and describes any ruling body, while regime often implies that the rulers are illegitimate or oppressive.
Regimen is a planned routine of diet, exercise or treatment; regime is broader and used more for political rule, though it is also used casually for routines.
Administration refers to a specific leader's term or team, such as the Biden administration, and is a neutral political term.

examples.everyday: I started a new morning workout regime, and I'm trying hard to stick to it.
examples.professional: Under the new regime, the finance team has to submit budget forecasts a week earlier than before.
examples.analytical: Historians debate whether the regime's propaganda or its economic policies did more to keep it in power.

nuance.analogy: Like a rulebook imposed from the top: rigid steps that everyone must follow whether they agree or not.
nuance.etymology: From Latin regimen 'rule, direction', from regere 'to rule, guide'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it REJ-uh-meen; the word is ruh-ZHEEM with a 'zh' sound.
Using regime for a diet or medical treatment plan, where regimen is more precise.
Using regime for any government; in American English it often implies a government that is illegitimate or oppressive.

regime.etymology: From Middle English *regime*, *regyme*, from Middle French *regime*, from Latin *regimen* (“direction, government”).

senses.definition: Overly strict; rigid.
Relating to a regiment.

core.definition: Of or relating to a military regiment; also, rigidly strict in the manner of military discipline.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on MEN, with a weaker secondary stress on the first syllable. The -ment ending is pronounced like 'ment', not 'mint', and the final -al is a reduced syllable, 'tul'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral when describing military units, such as regimental colors or history. Negative when used figuratively for rigid rules.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use regimental mostly in military or historical contexts, such as a regimental history or regimental insignia. The figurative sense of rigid or strict is rare in everyday speech and sounds stiff; for that, Americans say strict, rigid or regimented. Military veterans and collectors use the word most often.

distinctions.note: Regimental refers to a military regiment or its traits, while regimented describes anything forced into strict order, whether military or not.
Military is the broad term for armed forces, while regimental is narrower and refers to one specific regiment.

examples.everyday: My grandfather still keeps his regimental photo from the Korean War in a frame on the wall.
examples.professional: The lab's regimental sign-in rules feel excessive, but the security team insists on them after last year's breach.
examples.analytical: The regimental style of the reform reflected a belief that discipline alone could produce loyalty.

nuance.analogy: Like a team uniform: a regimental identity shows belonging to one specific unit within a larger army.
nuance.etymology: From regiment, from Latin regimentum 'rule, government', from regere 'to rule'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'REJ-uh-men-tul'; the main stress is on MEN.
Using regimental for any strict rule; in everyday American English, say strict or regimented instead.
Pronouncing the -ment as 'mint'.

senses.definition: Eligible for repayment, particularly for money spent or expenses incurred; qualifying for reimbursement.
senses.example: Buying a souvenir during a business trip is not a reimbursable expense.

senses.definition: Something the expense for which can be reimbursed.
senses.example: Only receipts for business travel are reimbursable under our company's expense policy.

core.definition: Eligible to be paid back, especially money you spent for work or travel that your employer, insurer, or another party will cover.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on burs, with the vowel of bur in a stressed position. The im- is light and the final syllables are reduced to uh-bul.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is practical business language with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use reimbursable in workplace, travel, and insurance contexts, especially in phrases like 'reimbursable expenses' on company policy pages. In casual talk people say you can get that paid back or the company will cover it. It is also used as a noun in some business writing.

distinctions.note: Refundable refers to money returned for something you paid for but did not get, while reimbursable refers to money you spent and are repaid.
Billable means charged to a client, while reimbursable means repaid to the person who paid the expense.

examples.everyday: Keep your cab receipt, because the fare is reimbursable.
examples.professional: Please send your hotel receipts, since mileage and meals are reimbursable under our travel policy.
examples.analytical: The contract separates reimbursable costs from fixed fees, which determines how the government audits each invoice.

nuance.analogy: Like a client dinner you pay for and then get back on your expense report.
nuance.etymology: From reimburse + -able; reimburse from Medieval Latin imbursare, from in- + bursa 'purse'.
common_mistakes: Misspelling it as reimbursible; the standard American spelling uses -able.
Using reimbursable as a verb or as a synonym for refundable in shopping situations.

senses.definition: To ease (a person, person's thoughts etc.) from mental distress; to stop (someone) feeling anxious or worried, to alleviate the distress of.
senses.example: I was greatly relieved by the jury's verdict.

senses.definition: To ease (someone, a part of the body etc.) or give relief from physical pain or discomfort.
To alleviate (pain, distress, mental discomfort etc.).
To provide comfort or assistance to (someone in need, especially in poverty).
To free (someone) from debt or legal obligations; to give legal relief to.
senses.example: This shall not relieve either Party of any obligations.

senses.definition: To bring military help to (a besieged town); to lift the siege on.
To release (someone) from or of a difficulty, unwanted task, responsibility etc.
To urinate or defecate.
To ease one's own desire to orgasm, often through masturbation to orgasm.
To free (someone) from their post, task etc. by taking their place.
(rare) To raise (someone) out of danger or from (a specified difficulty etc.).
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To make (something) stand out; to make prominent, bring into relief.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To ease someone's worry, anxiety, or physical pain, or to reduce the feeling of distress.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second and only stressed syllable, LEEV. The long e sound is clear, and the final v is voiced. Do not add a y sound between the syllables.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes helping someone feel better, whether from pain, stress, or a difficult situation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use relieve with feelings and pain: 'I'm relieved to hear that' or 'This cream relieves itching.' In everyday talk, 'help' or 'ease' may sound more natural, but relieve is standard in medical, professional, and formal writing. It is also used in the military and business for taking over a duty from someone.

distinctions.note: Ease is more general and gentle; relieve usually implies removing a specific pain, worry, or burden.
Comfort focuses on emotional support; relieve can refer to physical or mental distress, and it often means removing the cause.

examples.everyday: A hot shower always relieves my back pain after a long day at work.
examples.professional: The new process should relieve the backlog by automating the first round of approvals.
examples.analytical: Scripture speaks of God as one who relieves the burdened, which suggests that divine care addresses not only sin but the weight of human suffering.

nuance.analogy: To relieve is like lifting a heavy backpack off someone's shoulders: the weight is still there, but they can finally breathe.
nuance.etymology: From Old French relever, to raise again or lift up, from Latin relevare, to lift up or lighten.
common_mistakes: Using relieve with 'from' incorrectly; say 'relieve someone of a burden' or 'relieve pain', not 'relieve from pain'.
Mispronouncing the final sound as a z or leaving out the v; it is a clear v, like in leave.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the idea of relief often appears as rest, comfort, or deliverance from distress. The Greek word anapauo means to give rest or refresh, and Jesus uses it in Matthew 11:28, inviting the weary and heavy laden to come to him for rest. Second Thessalonians 1:7 uses the Greek word anesis, meaning relief or release, speaking of rest for those who are afflicted when the Lord is revealed.

relieve.etymology: From Late Middle English *releven*, from Old French *relever*, specifically from the conjugated forms such as *relieve* (“I lift up”), and its source, Latin *relevo* (“to lift up, lighten, relieve, alleviate”), combined form of *re-* (“back”) + *levo* (“to…

senses.definition: The quality of being remote.

core.definition: The state of being far away or isolated from other places or people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MOHT. Start with a clear ree sound, not 'reh', and do not pronounce the final -ness as a separate syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound peaceful in a travel or nature context and isolating in a social or economic one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use remoteness to describe places, such as rural towns, islands or mountain cabins, that are hard to reach. It can describe a feeling of being cut off from people. For everyday talk, people often say they live way out there or in the middle of nowhere.

distinctions.note: Distance measures how far apart things are, while remoteness suggests isolation or difficulty of access.
Isolation emphasizes being separated from others, while remoteness focuses more on location far from centers.

examples.everyday: We loved the remoteness of the cabin, but the cell signal was terrible.
examples.professional: The remoteness of our field offices makes it hard to send technicians on short notice.
examples.analytical: The remoteness of the monastery shaped its rhythm of prayer and its relative independence from court politics.

nuance.analogy: Remoteness is like a lighthouse on a faraway island, visible from the sea but far from the shore.
nuance.etymology: From remote (from Latin remotus, 'removed') plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in ree-MOHT-nis-s.
Confusing remoteness with remotely, which is an adverb.

senses.definition: To cause the memory of past trauma to be recalled, resulting in renewed suffering.
senses.example: Asking about her brother's accident would only reopen old wounds for my grieving mother.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see reopen,‎ old,‎ wound.

core.definition: To bring back painful memories, feelings, or conflicts from the past, causing renewed hurt between people.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on OH in reopen and on WOUNDS at the end. Old is a light word, so say it quickly and do not stress it as much as the other words.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes causing renewed pain, so people use it carefully and often in apologies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom about family arguments, divorces, past betrayals, and public events that revive trauma. A common phrase is 'I didn't mean to reopen old wounds.' Do not use it for minor annoyances, because it suggests real emotional pain.

distinctions.note: Bring up the past is neutral and can refer to any old topic. Reopen old wounds focuses on renewed emotional pain.
Dredge up suggests deliberately digging out something unpleasant, often in a critical way. Reopen old wounds focuses on the hurt that returns.

collocations: reopen old wounds in the family
reopen old wounds from the divorce
reopen old wounds of the war
prefer not to reopen old wounds

examples.everyday: I'd rather not bring up your brother's wedding, because I don't want to reopen old wounds.
examples.professional: Bringing up last year's layoffs in the planning meeting would reopen old wounds before we get to the new plan.
examples.analytical: Public apologies can reopen old wounds for victims, which is why many reconciliation processes prioritize private accounts.

nuance.analogy: A scar looks healed until a bump opens the cut again, and the pain returns as if it were new.
nuance.etymology: From reopen (re- plus open) and wound, from Old English wund.
common_mistakes: Using the idiom for a literal wound unless you mean the wound itself; for a physical wound, say 'the wound reopened.'
Using the idiom for small disagreements; it implies serious emotional harm.

senses.definition: To find a solution to (a problem).
To reduce to simple or intelligible notions; to make clear or certain; to unravel; to explain.
senses.example: to resolve a riddle

senses.definition: To make a firm decision to do something. To become determined to reach a certain goal or take a certain action.
senses.example: I resolve to finish this work before I go home.

senses.definition: To determine or decide in purpose; to make ready in mind; to fix; to settle.
senses.example: He was resolved by an unexpected event.

senses.definition: To come to an agreement or make peace; patch up relationship, settle differences, bury the hatchet.
senses.example: After two weeks of bickering, they finally resolved their differences.

senses.definition: To break down into constituent parts; to decompose; to disintegrate; to return to a simpler constitution or a primeval state.
senses.example: The House immediately resolved itself into a Committee on the Bill.

senses.definition: To cause to perceive or understand; to acquaint; to inform; to convince; to assure; to make certain.
senses.example: The engineer's detailed demonstration finally resolved the team that the system was safe.

senses.definition: To render visible or distinguishable the parts of something.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the fine lines of the sample resolved into distinct, separate grains.

senses.definition: To find the IP address of a hostname, or the entity referred to by a symbol in source code; to look up.
senses.example: Before connecting, the client must resolve the server's hostname to its current IP address.

senses.definition: To liquefy (a gas or vapor).
senses.example: The refinery compresses and cools the propane until it can resolve the vapor into liquid.

senses.definition: To cause a chord to go from dissonance to consonance.
senses.example: The composer resolved the dissonant chord into a bright major triad at the final cadence.

senses.definition: To separate racemic compounds into their enantiomers.
senses.example: The chemist used a chiral column to resolve the racemic mixture into its two enantiomers.

senses.definition: (rare) To melt; to dissolve; to liquefy or soften (a solid).
senses.example: After an hour in the sun, the butter began to resolve into a golden pool.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (rare) To melt; to dissolve; to become liquid.
senses.example: After an hour in the sun, the butter began to resolve into a golden pool.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: (dated) To disperse or scatter; to discuss, as an inflammation or a tumor.
senses.example: The surgeon hoped the warm compresses would resolve the swelling before any operation was needed.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Determination; will power.
senses.example: It took all my resolve to go through with the surgery.

senses.definition: A determination to do something; a fixed decision.
senses.example: Her resolve to finish the marathon never wavered, even in the freezing rain.

senses.definition: An act of resolving something; resolution.
senses.example: The quick resolve of the billing error saved me a lot of frustration.

core.definition: To find a solution to a problem or settle a disagreement so that it no longer exists.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the final -solve is a single short syllable, not 'sohlv'. Americans pronounce the o like the a in 'father', so 'resolve' and 'solve' sound alike except for the stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it implies that something difficult has been fixed or settled. The sense of firmly deciding is also positive, suggesting strength of purpose.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'resolve' for problems, conflicts, and disputes, as in 'resolve the issue' or 'resolve the dispute'. For personal decisions, they say 'I resolved to start running' or 'I'm resolved to finish this', which sounds a little formal or literary in casual speech. In daily talk, 'fix' or 'sort out' is more common for everyday problems.

distinctions.note: 'Solve' is used for problems with a definite answer, like equations or puzzles, while 'resolve' is used for conflicts, disputes, or uncertainties that need to be settled.
'Settle' is more informal and often implies that both sides agreed, whereas 'resolve' can describe a neutral or official outcome.
'Determine' means to establish a fact or decide something by investigation, while 'resolve' focuses on ending a problem or reaching a decision.

examples.everyday: I finally resolved the billing mix-up with the phone company this morning.
examples.professional: Let's resolve the schema conflict before the Monday release so the dashboards don't break.
examples.analytical: Kant tries to resolve the conflict between determinism and moral freedom by distinguishing appearances from things in themselves.

nuance.analogy: Like untying a knot, you loosen each strand until the tangle comes apart.
nuance.etymology: From Latin resolvere, 'to loosen, untie, dissolve'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'resolve about the issue' instead of 'resolve the issue', because 'resolve' takes a direct object.
Using 'resolve' for simple questions with clear answers, where 'solve' or 'answer' is more natural.

resolve.etymology: From Middle English *resolven*, from Old French *resolver*, a learned borrowing of Latin *resolvō* (“loosen, thaw, melt, resolve”), equivalent to *re* + *solve*.

senses.definition: The act of resuscitating.
senses.example: Quick resuscitation with oxygen and chest compressions saved the swimmer's life.

core.definition: The act of reviving someone who has stopped breathing or whose heart has stopped, usually using CPR or other emergency methods.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on -TAY-, and the first syllables are short and unstressed. Many learners pronounce the middle syllables too clearly, so say rih-suh-sih quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in medical contexts, but it carries urgency and drama in emergency situations.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in medical, emergency and news contexts, such as hospital reports or news about a rescue. In everyday talk people often say CPR or say someone was brought back. The word is also used figuratively for reviving a failing business or program, though this is less common.

distinctions.note: CPR, cardiopulmonary resuscitation, is one specific procedure; resuscitation is the broader act of reviving someone, which may include other methods.
Revival usually means renewed interest or energy; resuscitation, in its literal sense, means restoring vital functions like breathing or heartbeat.
Rescue means removing someone from danger; resuscitation means restoring life functions after they have stopped.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is a nurse, so she started resuscitation right away when her husband collapsed in the yard.
examples.professional: The hospital's new protocol shortens the time before resuscitation begins after a cardiac arrest.
examples.analytical: Ethicists debate how long resuscitation should continue when the chance of neurological recovery is very small.

nuance.analogy: Like jump-starting a dead car battery: the goal is to restart a system that has stopped.
nuance.etymology: From Latin resuscitare, 'to raise up again', from re- ('again') and suscitare ('to rouse, raise').
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying ree-suh-SIH-tay-shun instead of rih-suh-sih-TAY-shun
Using it for a person's energy after a long day; in that case say a pick-me-up or revival

resuscitation.etymology: From Middle English *resuscitacion*, from Old French *ressuscitacion* and Latin *resuscitātio*.

senses.definition: The transfer of risk from one reinsurer to another.
The return of land, rights, etc. previously ceded.
Metastasis of an eruption or tumor from the surface to the interior of the body.
senses.example: The oncologist noted a retrocession of the melanoma from the skin into the internal organs.

senses.definition: The act of retroceding; a going back.
senses.example: The committee approved the retrocession of the disputed territory back to its former owner.

core.definition: In insurance, the passing of part of a reinsurer's risk on to another reinsurer. In general use, the return of land or rights previously transferred.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, SESH. The final -ion is a weak syllable, so say 'un'. The sh sound is a clear American 'sh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet this word in insurance and reinsurance contracts and in legal or historical writing. In everyday talk it is rare, and people would say 'return' or 'transfer back'. It is a specialist term and should be used carefully.

distinctions.note: Cession is the original transfer of risk or property; retrocession is a transfer passed back or onward from that first recipient.
Retrocession is the more common term in insurance; the other form is much rarer and less standard in American usage.

examples.everyday: My uncle works in insurance, and he said the company buys retrocession to protect itself from big losses.
examples.professional: We reviewed the retrocession treaty to see how much of the catastrophe exposure we could pass to other reinsurers.
examples.analytical: Retrocession chains can obscure the ultimate holder of risk, which complicates regulatory oversight of the reinsurance market.

nuance.analogy: Retrocession is like a restaurant passing an extra-large order to another kitchen so that no single kitchen is overwhelmed.
nuance.etymology: From Latin retrocedere, to go back, from retro, backward, and cedere, to yield or go.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'retrocession' with 'recession', the economic term.
Using it for everyday returns of goods, where 'return' is the normal word.

senses.definition: To value again, give a new value to.

core.definition: To assign a new value to something, such as a currency, asset, property, or company, by officially checking its worth again.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, val. The final syllable is yoo, a full vowel, so do not say it as 'ya' or add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a formal change in worth and does not carry a built-in judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use revalue mainly in finance, accounting, real estate, and formal writing. In everyday talk, people usually say reassess or appraise again, especially for a house. For an idea or opinion, say reconsider or rethink rather than revalue.

distinctions.note: Reassess means judge something again in general, while revalue specifically assigns a new numerical or monetary worth.
Devalue lowers worth, and it can also mean to make someone feel less important, while revalue is neutral about the direction of change.

examples.everyday: The appraiser came out to revalue our house before we refinanced.
examples.professional: We need to revalue the inventory at current market prices before the quarterly report.
examples.analytical: Economists disagree about whether a government should revalue its currency when its trade surplus keeps growing.

nuance.analogy: Like a store updating every price tag after a sudden change in costs, so each item gets a new value.
nuance.etymology: From re- (again) plus value, from Latin valere, to be worth.
common_mistakes: Using revalue for opinions or ideas; say reconsider or rethink in everyday talk.
Stressing the last syllable as ree-val-YOO, which is not the American stress pattern.

senses.definition: To regard someone or something with great awe or devotion.
senses.example: a highly revered musician

senses.definition: To honor in a form lesser than worship, e.g. a saint, or an idol.
senses.example: Many Catholics revere saints, asking them to intercede in prayer.

senses.definition: A revers.

core.definition: To feel deep respect and admiration for someone or something, often bordering on awe.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the second syllable. The vowel is a long 'ee' with a clear American r, so do not drop the r or turn it into 'ruh-VEE.' Do not confuse it with 'revers,' the lapel.

nuance.connotation: Positive; suggests high respect, often for people, traditions, or achievements.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use revere in formal speech, writing, and ceremonies, for example 'we revere our founders.' In casual conversation people usually say 'admire,' 'respect,' or 'look up to.' It can sound stiff when used for ordinary people.

distinctions.note: Admire is everyday and focuses on approval or liking; revere implies a deeper, almost sacred respect.
Worship is religious devotion to God; revere can describe respect for people or ideas without religious meaning.

examples.everyday: My grandmother was revered in our family for her cooking and her stories.
examples.professional: Our engineers revere the original architects, but they also want to rebuild the system.
examples.analytical: Many Christians revere the saints as witnesses to the faith, though the degree of honor varies.

nuance.analogy: To revere something is to hold it like a lit candle: carefully, with respect and warmth.
nuance.etymology: From Latin revereri, 'to stand in awe of,' from re- and vereri (to fear, respect).
common_mistakes: Confusing revere (to respect) with revers (a lapel), which is a different word.
Using revere for casual admiration, which can sound too formal.

senses.definition: Advocacy for the revival of a former practice, custom, etc.
senses.example: Art Deco revivalism

senses.definition: Spiritual fervor of or for a religious revival.

core.definition: The movement or belief that promotes religious revival, emphasizing emotional conversion, renewed commitment, and evangelistic meetings.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on VY, the second syllable. The ending -ism is unstressed and sounds like iz-um, so avoid stressing the final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mixed: supporters see it as renewing faith, while critics may see emotional excess or manipulation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use revivalism mainly in religious history, theology, and academic writing about movements such as the Second Great Awakening. In church conversation people usually say revival or revival meetings. Calling someone a revivalist can be mild criticism, implying emotional pressure.

distinctions.note: A revival is an event or period of renewal, while revivalism is the ideology or movement that promotes such events.
Fundamentalism stresses strict doctrinal literalism, while revivalism stresses conversion experience and renewal of personal faith.
Nostalgia is a sentiment about the past, while revivalism is an organized effort to restore a practice or spirit.

examples.everyday: My uncle got swept up in some revivalism at his church and now goes to three prayer meetings a week.
examples.professional: The conference panel discussed how modern church planters draw on older revivalism while avoiding its emotional excesses.
examples.analytical: Charles Finney's revivalism reframed conversion as a decision that humans make, shifting Protestant understanding of grace and responsibility.

nuance.analogy: Revival is the tide coming back in, while revivalism is the organized campaign that tries to call the tide in.
nuance.etymology: From revival with the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using revivalism as a synonym for a single revival meeting; it names the movement or ideology.
Stressing the final syllable as -IZ-um; the main stress stays on VY.

senses.definition: Someone who seeks to revive something.
senses.example: an Art Deco revivalist

senses.definition: An evangelistic preacher.
Evangelistic.
senses.example: The revivalist preacher filled the tent with shouting and singing every evening all summer.

core.definition: A preacher or leader who holds revival meetings to renew religious faith and call people to conversion.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, VYE. The final -ist is short, and the middle syllable is weak, so say 'vuh-list' quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in religious history; positive among supporters and negative among critics who see manipulative emotionalism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use revivalist mainly for Protestant preachers, especially in the Great Awakenings or in evangelical and camp-meeting traditions. Today evangelist is the common everyday term, and revivalist sounds historical. You might hear someone say 'a traditional revivalist' when describing a preacher with a tent meeting style.

distinctions.note: An evangelist preaches the gospel to win outsiders; a revivalist focuses on renewing the faith of believers through meetings.
A reformer changes church structure or doctrine; a revivalist aims at spiritual renewal and personal commitment.

examples.everyday: My grandmother still talks about the traveling revivalist who preached under a tent outside town.
examples.professional: The church hired a revivalist to lead a weeklong series of evening services.
examples.analytical: Nineteenth-century revivalists reshaped American religion by making personal conversion the center of worship.

nuance.analogy: Like a fire-starter who wakes up embers in a cold stove.
nuance.etymology: From revival plus -ist; revive comes from Late Latin revivere, to come back to life.
common_mistakes: Using revivalist for any leader of a movement; in religion it means a preacher who holds revival meetings.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'REE-vye-vuh-list'.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture does not use the word revivalist, but the idea of renewal behind it is the Hebrew verb chayah, meaning to live or to revive. Psalm 85:6 asks whether God will not revive his people again, and Psalm 71:20 speaks of God reviving the psalmist after trouble. Ezra 9:8-9 describes a little reviving of the returned exiles through God's favor.

traditions.view: Renewal comes through the sacramental life and liturgy of the Church rather than through campaign-style meetings; revival is understood as the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit within the Church.

Renewal is pursued through the sacraments, parish missions, retreats, and charismatic renewal groups, with caution toward emotional campaigns that bypass the Church's teaching and sacramental structure.

Evangelicals, Methodists, and Pentecostals have long valued revival meetings as a means of conversion and renewal, while Lutheran and Reformed churches have been more cautious and Anglicans often emphasize liturgy.

senses.definition: Rhyming verse (poetic form).
senses.example: Many editors say they don’t want stories written in rhyme these days.

senses.definition: A thought expressed in verse; a verse; a poem; a tale told in verse.
senses.example: Tennyson’s rhymes

senses.definition: A word that rhymes with another.
senses.example: Norse poetry is littered with rhymes like “sól … sunnan”.

senses.definition: A word that rhymes with another, in that it is pronounced identically with the other word from the vowel in its stressed syllable to the end.
senses.example: "Awake" is a rhyme for "lake".

senses.definition: Rhyming: sameness of letters or sounds of part of some words.
senses.example: The poem exhibits a peculiar form of rhyme.

senses.definition: The second part of a syllable, from the vowel on, as opposed to the onset.
senses.example: Linguists analyze the rhyme of a syllable, which in cat is the vowel and final consonant.

senses.definition: An instance of rapping; a rapped verse; a line or couple lines of rapping; a hip hop song.
senses.example: I heard Drake's new rhyme last night.

senses.definition: A rapper's oeuvre, lyricism or skill.
