senses.example: His rhymes are all weak.

senses.definition: To compose or treat in verse; versify.
senses.example: She loved to rhyme her poems about the ocean and the changing seasons.

senses.definition: To place in such a way as to produce a rhyme or an approximation thereof.
senses.example: Try to rhyme the lines so the chorus ends with home and alone.

senses.definition: Of a word, to be pronounced identically with another from the vowel in its stressed syllable to the end.
senses.example: Creation rhymes with integration and station.

senses.definition: To be pronounced identically from the vowel in the stressed syllable of each to the end of each.
senses.example: Mug and rug rhyme.

senses.definition: To contain words that are pronounced identically to each other from the vowel in the stressed syllable to the end.
senses.example: I rewrote the story to make it rhyme.

senses.definition: To somewhat resemble or correspond with.
senses.example: His explanation doesn't rhyme with the evidence we found in the financial records.

core.definition: Words that end with the same sounds, starting from the stressed vowel, such as 'cat' and 'hat'; or a short poem using such words.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with the diphthong of 'time' and 'climb'. The h is silent, so do not add an aspirated sound at the start.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in poetry, rhyme is a positive craft feature, but in everyday talk it is simply descriptive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'rhyme' both for matching word endings and for a short verse, such as a nursery rhyme. The idiom 'without rhyme or reason' means without any logic or sense, and people say it casually about confusing decisions. Children learn rhymes early, so the word is very common in classrooms and at home.

distinctions.note: Rhythm is the pattern of stressed and unstressed beats over time; rhyme is the matching of sounds at the ends of words.
Verse is any line of poetry, rhymed or not; rhyme is only one feature that verse may have.

examples.everyday: My kid keeps making up silly rhymes about our dog, like 'Max' and 'tracks'.
examples.professional: The tagline with a rhyme tested better with our focus group than the longer slogan did.
examples.analytical: A perfect rhyme requires an identical stressed vowel and identical sounds after it, not merely similar sounds.

nuance.analogy: Like two puzzle pieces whose edges match, so the endings fit together even though the words are different.
nuance.etymology: From Old French rime, possibly from Latin rhythmus; the spelling was later altered in English to match rhythm.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the silent h at the start of rhyme.
Confusing rhyme with rhythm, which is about beat rather than matching word endings.

rhyme.etymology: From Middle English *rim*, *rime*, *ryme* (“identical letters or sounds in words from the vowel in their stressed syllables to their ends; measure, meter, rhythm; song, verse, etc. with rhyming lines”), from Anglo-Norman *rime*, *ryme* (“identical letters…

senses.definition: A path cut through woodland.
senses.example: We followed a narrow riding through the forest until it opened onto a sunny meadow.

senses.definition: The act of one who rides; a mounted excursion.
senses.example: Her morning riding along the coast trail cleared her head before work.

senses.definition: The behavior in the motion of a vehicle, such as oscillation.
senses.example: The suspension upgrade improved the riding of the van on gravel roads.

senses.definition: Electoral district or constituency.
senses.example: The senator has held the riding for twelve years and expects a tough reelection campaign.

senses.definition: (historical) A festival procession.
senses.example: Medieval townsfolk gathered along the streets for the riding, singing and carrying painted banners.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) Any of the three administrative divisions of Yorkshire and some other northern counties of England.
senses.example: The historian traced the boundaries of the North Riding in the medieval records.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: The sport or activity of riding horses, often for pleasure or competition.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on RY, and the second syllable is a short, reduced 'ding'. Keep the vowel in ride long and clear, and avoid adding an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests hobbies, outdoor life, and recreation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say riding for horseback riding, especially in phrases like 'go riding' or 'riding lessons'. In a general sense, riding can also mean the act of riding a bicycle or motorcycle, but for a bike people more often say 'biking' or 'cycling'. For a path through the woods, Americans typically say trail, not riding.

distinctions.note: Horseback riding is the more explicit phrase, while riding is shorter and common in casual conversation about horses.
Equestrian is more formal and technical, referring to the sport or skills of horsemanship, while riding is everyday language.

examples.everyday: My daughter has been taking riding lessons every Saturday since spring.
examples.professional: The riding program at the camp needs a new instructor and updated insurance coverage.
examples.analytical: For the medieval knight, riding was less a pastime than a discipline that shaped his moral identity.

nuance.analogy: Like learning to play an instrument, riding combines physical balance with a partner who has a will of its own.
nuance.etymology: From ride (Old English rīdan) with the -ing suffix.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I go to riding' instead of 'I go riding'; the verb is used without 'to' here.
Confusing riding with the verb ride when a noun is needed, as in 'I like riding' versus 'I like to ride'.

senses.definition: To ascend to the surface.
senses.example: Bubbles rise up from the bottom of the pot as the water heats.

senses.definition: To mount a rebellion or insurgency; to rebel; to revolt.
Of a horse, etc. to rear.
senses.example: The stallion began to rise up on its hind legs, startling the riders.

core.definition: To stand up or to move upward; or, to rebel or revolt against a person or system in power.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on up, the particle, as usual in phrasal verbs. The first word, rise, has a light secondary stress, and the final p is released clearly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in literal use, but negative or strongly charged when it means rebellion or revolt.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rise up for water or waves that move upward, but it is most often used for a group that rebels against authority, as in people rise up against an unfair regime. In workplaces it can mean a group of employees refusing to accept something. It sounds dramatic, so Americans use it more in news, history and fiction than in everyday speech.

distinctions.note: Revolt is a more formal and general word for a rebellion, while rise up is more dramatic and often used about people spontaneously standing up together.
Rebel can describe a single person who refuses authority, while rise up usually describes a group or crowd.

examples.everyday: The waves rose up over the pier during the storm, and everyone ran to higher ground.
examples.professional: Junior engineers rose up and asked for clearer deadlines, and leadership responded with a new planning process.
examples.analytical: Marx argued that the oppressed classes must rise up to overthrow the economic structures that exploit them.

nuance.analogy: Rise up is like a tide that starts small and gathers strength until it crashes over the wall.
common_mistakes: Using raise up with a person as the object, which is a different verb: raise up leaders is not the same as rise up against them.
Adding against without the verb: people rise up against the government is correct, but rise up the government is not.

senses.definition: A person who serves as an example, or whose behavior is emulated by others.

core.definition: A person whose behavior, character or achievements other people admire and want to imitate.

pronunciation.tip: In this compound noun, the main stress falls on ROLE, and 'model' is lighter with a syllabic l at the end. Don't pronounce it 'mo-dell' or give both words equal stress.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it describes someone admirable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'role model' often in schools, sports, workplaces and family conversation, as in 'She's a great role model for kids.' It is standard in speech and writing. A natural reply is 'Yeah, she really is' or 'I look up to her too'.

distinctions.note: A mentor advises you directly and personally; a role model can be admired from a distance.
An idol is admired so intensely it can border on worship; a role model is a measured and practical example.
An example illustrates a point; a role model is a person whose life others want to follow.

collocations: set a good example as a role model
look up to a role model

examples.everyday: My grandmother was my role model; she worked two jobs and never complained.
examples.professional: Our senior engineer is a great role model for new hires who want to write clean code.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of virtue suggests that role models shape character by making excellence visible in practice.

nuance.analogy: A lighthouse: people steer by its light without the light steering them.
nuance.etymology: Role from French rôle combined with model from Latin modulus, a measure; a modern English compound.
common_mistakes: Giving equal stress to both words; the compound stress falls on ROLE.
Using 'role model' for anyone you simply know; it implies someone worth imitating.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the idea of a pattern for others to follow. The Greek word typos means pattern or example, as in 1 Timothy 4:12, where Paul urges Timothy to set believers an example in speech, conduct, love, faith and purity. In 1 Corinthians 11:1, Paul tells believers to imitate him as he imitates Christ, and Philippians 3:17 similarly asks readers to follow those who live by the example they have received.

senses.definition: Prayer beads, a string of beads used to keep track of repetitions in prayer, particularly of the Roman Catholic Marian prayer "Hail Mary" (Ave Maria).

A Roman Catholic devotion involving the repetition of a series of Marian prayers, usually 5, 15, or 20 decades of "Hail Marys", each decade beginning with "Our Father" and ending with "Glory Be to the Father", but sometimes including other Roman Catholic, Anglican, or Lutheran prayers.
A series or collection of thoughts, literary pieces, etc. intended for similar contemplation.
A rose garden.
(historical) A 13th-century coin minted in Europe as a counterfeit debased form of the sterling silver penny of Edward I, at first accepted as a halfpenny and then outlawed.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A string of prayer beads used to count repeated prayers, especially in Roman Catholic devotion, or the set of prayers said with them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle syllable to a quick uh. The final syllable is a light ree, and the r is clearly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to respectful; in Catholic settings it is a sacred practice, and in other settings it may be seen as a devotional object.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rosary for the beads and for the prayer practice, mostly in Catholic families, parishes and devotional contexts. Saying you pray the rosary is a normal, respectful thing to say, and in secular contexts it is simply a word for prayer beads. A natural reply is 'That's beautiful, my grandmother prayed the rosary every night.'

distinctions.note: Prayer beads is a general term for beads used in many religions, while rosary specifically refers to the Catholic beads and prayer pattern.
A prayer rope is used in Eastern Orthodox practice, usually for the Jesus Prayer, and has knots rather than the Catholic decade structure.

collocations: the Sorrowful Mysteries of the rosary

examples.everyday: My aunt always has her rosary in her purse when we visit the church.
examples.professional: The parish is hosting a rosary group on Tuesdays for members who want to pray together.
examples.analytical: The rosary combines vocal prayer and meditation on the life of Christ, which shapes its theological meaning in Catholic devotion.

nuance.analogy: A rosary is like a counting device for prayer, similar to a tally on a clicker, but with each bead carrying a prayer.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rosarium, meaning rose garden, a sense linked to the image of roses in Marian devotion.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable too strongly, as ROH-zair-ee; the middle syllable is reduced.
Using rosary as a verb; Americans say pray the rosary or say the rosary.

traditions.view: The rosary is a Marian devotion that repeats the Hail Mary, the Our Father and the Glory Be while meditating on the mysteries of Christ's life, and it is encouraged as a form of prayer.
Orthodox Christians use prayer ropes or knotted cords, often for the Jesus Prayer, and do not follow the Catholic rosary pattern or the Marian prayers in the same way.
Most Protestants do not use the rosary, regarding Marian prayers and repetitive prayer patterns with suspicion, though some Anglicans and Lutherans use prayer beads for personal devotion.

rosary.etymology: From Middle English *rosarie*, from Latin *rosārium*, here in its sense as a garland of roses.

senses.definition: A circular frill or ruffle on a garment, especially a starched, fluted frill at the neck in Elizabethan and Jacobean England (1560s–1620s).
senses.example: Elizabethan portraits often show nobles wearing a large starched ruff at the neck.

senses.definition: Anything formed with plaits or flutings like a frill.
senses.example: The pastry chef piped a ruff of frilled dough around the edge of the tart.

senses.definition: Senses relating to animals.

A gregarious, medium-sized wading bird of species Calidris pugnax (syn. Philomachus pugnax), of Eurasia; specifically, a male of the species which develops a distinctive ruff of feathers and ear tufts during mating season (the female is called a reeve).
senses.example: We spotted a male ruff in the flooded field, its feathers puffed out for courtship.

senses.definition: A collar on a shaft or other piece to prevent endwise motion.
senses.example: Slide the ruff onto the shaft before tightening the bolt to stop it sliding.

senses.definition: A fish of species Arripis georgianus, found in cool waters off the southern coast of Australia.
senses.example: Anglers off South Australia's coast often catch a ruff while fishing for snapper.

senses.definition: An instance of ruffing, or an opportunity to ruff, when unable to follow suit.
senses.example: He had no clubs left, so he took the trick with a ruff.

senses.definition: A set of lengthened or otherwise modified feathers on or around the neck of a bird.
senses.example: The rooster's ruff of long feathers stood up when the dog barked.

senses.definition: A collar of lengthened or distinctively colored fur on or around the neck of an animal.
senses.example: The wolf's thick ruff of fur made it look larger in the snow.

senses.definition: A low, vibrating beat of a drum, quieter than a roll; a ruffle.
senses.example: The drummer began with a soft ruff before the singer walked onto the stage.

senses.definition: To shape (fabric, etc.) into a ruff; to adorn (a garment, etc.) with a ruff.
senses.example: She ruffed the collar of the costume with starched linen for the play.

senses.definition: Of a falcon, hawk, etc.: to hit (the prey) without fixing or grabbing hold of it.
senses.example: The falcon ruffed the pigeon in midair but failed to grab it.

senses.definition: To play a trump card to a trick when unable to follow suit (that is, when unable to play a card of the same suit as the previous or leading card).
senses.example: With no spades left, she ruffed the diamond with a trump and won the trick.

senses.definition: Especially in the form ruff out: to defeat (a card, etc.) by ruffing, thus establishing the master card in the suit led.
senses.example: She ruffed out the opponent's ace, establishing her last club as the master card.

senses.definition: To beat a ruff or ruffle, as on a drum.
senses.example: The drummer ruffed softly on the snare while the crowd fell silent.

senses.definition: Of a drum, etc.: to have a ruff or ruffle beaten on it.
senses.example: The snare drum was ruffed at the start of the funeral procession.

senses.definition: (rare) To ruffle; to disorder.
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: The bark of a dog; arf, woof.

core.definition: The short, sharp sound a dog makes when barking, often repeated as 'ruff, ruff' in children's speech and books.

pronunciation.tip: Use the short 'uh' vowel of 'cup' or 'stuff,' not the 'oo' of 'roof.' Keep the sound clipped and end it with a sharp 'f.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and playful. It is mostly used with children or to imitate a dog.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually imitate a dog's bark with 'woof' or 'arf,' and 'ruff' is more common in children's books, baby talk and cartoons. Adults use it playfully, for example 'Our puppy went ruff, ruff at the mail carrier.' In formal writing you would describe a bark rather than use this sound word.

distinctions.note: 'Woof' is the most common American imitation of a dog's bark for adults and children, while 'ruff' is more childlike and sounds more like a small dog.
'Arf' is a cartoonish sound, often used for a larger or more playful dog, while 'ruff' is closer to a plain bark.

examples.everyday: The puppy ran to the door and went ruff, ruff! when the mail came.
examples.professional: For the kids' reading program, we will use the word 'ruff' to teach animal sounds, and then compare it to the sounds in other languages.
examples.analytical: Words like 'ruff' show how speakers shape animal sounds through their own phonology, so English speakers and speakers of other languages hear the same bark differently.

nuance.analogy: A ruff is like a small, sharp knock on a door: short, quick and meant to get attention.
nuance.etymology: Imitative of a dog's bark.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with the 'oo' vowel of 'roof' or 'rough.'
Confusing the dog sound 'ruff' with the card term 'ruff' or the historical collar 'ruff.'
Using 'ruff' as a standard adult word for a dog's bark in formal English; 'bark' or 'woof' is more natural.

senses.definition: To reject an option from a list of possibilities.
senses.example: As Jane Doe had an alibi, the police were able to rule her out as a suspect.

senses.definition: To cross an item out by drawing a straight line through it, as with a ruler.
senses.example: She ruled out the duplicate entries by drawing a line through each one.

senses.definition: To make something impossible.
senses.example: The constant rain ruled out any chance of a game of tennis.

senses.definition: To disallow.
senses.example: The judge ruled out the confession because police had not read his rights.

senses.definition: To make unavailable.
senses.example: The sudden storm ruled out a trip to the beach for the entire weekend.

core.definition: To decide that something is not possible or should not be considered, or to eliminate an option.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on "out," with a light secondary stress on "rule." Say "rool-OWT," and do not put strong stress on "rule."

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a decision to exclude something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use "rule out" in everyday talk about medical tests, plans, and decisions, such as "The doctor ruled out an infection." It is often used in negative or open-ended ways. A natural reply might be "Okay, so that's off the table."

distinctions.note: "Exclude" is more formal and emphasizes leaving something out of a group; "rule out" is common in everyday decisions.
"Eliminate" often means to remove completely; "rule out" means to decide something is not an option, which may be temporary.

examples.everyday: The mechanic ruled out a flat tire, so it must be the battery.
examples.professional: We have ruled out a server failure, so the bug is probably in the client code.
examples.analytical: The historian ruled out economic motives, though the evidence remains incomplete.

nuance.analogy: Ruling out an option is like crossing names off a guest list until only the right people are left.
nuance.etymology: From rule (to decide or determine) plus out, meaning to exclude or reject.
common_mistakes: Saying "rule out of" with an extra preposition.
Putting heavy stress on "rule" instead of "out."

conversation.text: The doctor ruled out a broken bone.
I wouldn't rule it out; anything can happen.

senses.definition: Bound by rules; rigidly uncompromising.

core.definition: Strictly bound by rules and procedures, often to the point of being inflexible when flexibility is needed.

pronunciation.tip: 'Bound' rhymes with 'found' and 'sound', not with 'bind'. The main stress falls on 'bound', and 'rule' has lighter secondary stress.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative. It is often used to criticize bureaucracies or people who refuse to adapt, though it can be neutral when describing consistency.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in workplace complaints, news about government agencies, and general criticism of rigid institutions. Saying someone is 'rule-bound' can sound like a complaint. If you want a positive meaning, say 'principled' or 'consistent' instead.

distinctions.note: Bureaucratic focuses on the organization and paperwork, while rule-bound focuses on rigid obedience to rules themselves.
Inflexible is a general word for not bending, while rule-bound specifically describes a commitment to rules over common sense.
Principled is a positive word for acting on firm values, whereas rule-bound often implies a lack of judgment.

examples.everyday: My landlord is so rule-bound that he won't even let us hang a picture without filling out a form.
examples.professional: Our rule-bound approval process slows down even small changes that pose no real risk.
examples.analytical: Weber's ideal bureaucracy can become rule-bound, pursuing its procedures even after they have stopped serving their original purpose.

nuance.analogy: A rule-bound person is like a GPS that insists on the original route even after the road is closed.
nuance.etymology: Rule, from Old French reule, joined with bound, the past participle of bind, meaning restricted.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'bound' as 'bind', which rhymes with 'find' rather than 'found'.
Using 'rule-bound' as a neutral compliment when Americans usually hear it as criticism.

senses.definition: The smallest animal of a litter.
The smallest child in the family.
senses.example: the runt of the family

senses.definition: Undersized or stunted plant, animal or person.
An uninfluential or unimportant person; a nobody.
An Ethernet packet that does not meet the medium's minimum packet size of 64 bytes.
A single word (or portion of a hyphenated word) that appears as the last line of a paragraph.
A breed of pigeon related to the carrier pigeon.
A bow.

core.definition: The smallest, weakest animal in a litter, or an informal word for a very small or weak person.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a short, relaxed u vowel. Do not add a second vowel after the n, and keep the t crisp at the end.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It can sound harsh or insulting when used of a person, though people use it casually about animals.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'the runt of the litter' for the smallest puppy or piglet, which is neutral. Calling a person a runt is informal and can be rude, so avoid it at work or in polite conversation. Among friends it may be a joking insult about someone's height.

distinctions.note: Shrimp is a casual, often playful term for a short person; runt is harsher and suggests someone weak or underdeveloped.
Midget is offensive and should be avoided; runt is an informal word for an animal or a small, weak person.

examples.everyday: That little puppy was the runt of the litter, but now she's the bravest one in the yard.
examples.professional: The team's smallest project was the runt, but it still shipped on time.
examples.analytical: Early theories of evolution treated the weakest individual as a runt, but later research showed that size alone does not explain survival.

nuance.analogy: A runt is like the last apple left on the tree, small and easy to overlook.
nuance.etymology: Middle English runt, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using runt as a polite word for a short adult, which sounds insulting in American English.
Pronouncing the vowel like the oo in 'root' instead of the short u in 'run.'

runt.etymology: The OED classifies this word as "of origin".

senses.definition: An attempt to come to conclusions despite incomplete information and possibly due to a preexisting bias.
senses.example: Rather than collecting the facts, it was a rush to judgment on the part of the department's leaders.

senses.definition: Synonym of jump to conclusions.
senses.example: Let's not rush to judgment about the missing funds until the audit is finished.

core.definition: Deciding that someone is guilty or that something is true before you have enough evidence, often because of bias.

pronunciation.tip: Stress JUJ in judgment, and link rush to the next word so it sounds like 'rush-tuh.' American judgment is spelled without the e and pronounced with a reduced final syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies unfairness, carelessness or bias, especially in news, law and public debate.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase in news, politics, sports and legal discussions when someone reaches a conclusion too quickly. A natural reply is 'Let's wait for the facts' or 'Fair point, let's slow down.' In the past tense, Americans may say 'They rushed to judgment,' which is a natural use of the phrase as a verb.

distinctions.note: Jump to conclusions is more casual and focuses on drawing a conclusion without thinking; rush to judgment is more formal and often implies a serious judgment about someone.
Prejudge means to form an opinion before the facts are known; rush to judgment describes the hasty act of deciding that happens as a result.

collocations: rush to judgment in the case

examples.everyday: Let's wait for the facts before we rush to judgment about what happened at the game.
examples.professional: Before we blame the vendor, let's not rush to judgment; the logs haven't been checked yet.
examples.analytical: Historians warn against a rush to judgment when they evaluate testimony recorded under political pressure.

nuance.analogy: Rushing to judgment is like reading the last page of a mystery and naming the killer before the detective has looked at the evidence.
nuance.etymology: Rush from Middle English russhen, and judgment from Old French jugement.
common_mistakes: Spelling it judgement, which is common in British English, but American writing uses judgment.
Saying 'rush to a judgment' with an article, which sounds unnatural in standard American usage.

senses.definition: The quality of being rustic.
That which makes something rustic.
senses.example: Visitors loved the rusticity of the farmhouse, with its exposed beams and handmade quilts.

core.definition: The quality of being rustic, meaning simple, plain, natural and unsophisticated, like country life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, stis. Keep the first syllable weak and the final ity as a short ee-like sound.

nuance.connotation: Often positive, suggesting charm and honesty. It can be negative if it implies crudeness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rusticity in writing about design, food, art, or people when they want to describe a simple, earthy quality. It sounds elevated, so in conversation many Americans would say rustic instead. Saying that a restaurant has a rustic feel is far more natural than talking about its rusticity.

distinctions.note: Rustic is the adjective used in everyday English, while rusticity names the abstract quality.
Simplicity is neutral and general, while rusticity specifically refers to country-like or earthy plainness.

examples.everyday: I love the rusticity of the old farmhouse, with its wooden beams and worn floors.
examples.professional: The brand wants to keep the rusticity of its packaging while improving the product's quality.
examples.analytical: The poet's rusticity is deliberate, as he sets the plain speech of farm laborers against the polished rhetoric of the court.

nuance.analogy: Rusticity is like a homemade loaf of bread with a rough crust: it is simple and honest, not polished or perfect.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rusticitas, from rusticus, rural, plus the English suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Using rusticity in casual conversation where rustic is more natural.
Confusing rusticity with rustication, which refers to a stay in the country.

senses.definition: A year of rest for the land observed every seven years in ancient Judea, which included allowing the fields to lie without tilling, sowing, or reaping from one autumn to the next in accordance with a Levitical commandment.
senses.example: The ancient Israelites were commanded to let their fields lie fallow during the sabbatical year.

senses.definition: A leave, often with full or half pay granted (as every seventh year) to one holding an administrative or professional position for rest, travel, or research.
senses.example: After seven years at the university, she took a sabbatical year to write and travel.

core.definition: In ancient Israel, every seventh year, when the land was left unplanted and debts were released, as commanded in Leviticus.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on BAT, not on the first syllable. The final syllable of sabbatical is reduced to a light kul sound, and year is pronounced as one syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in the everyday American sense it suggests a respected, earned break.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, sabbatical most often means a paid leave that professors and some professionals take, often after several years of service, for research or rest. The biblical sense is mainly used in religious study or teaching. Americans usually say 'on sabbatical' or 'take a sabbatical' rather than naming the year.

distinctions.note: A vacation is a short break from work, while a sabbatical is a longer leave, often months, for study or renewal.
A jubilee is every fiftieth year in Leviticus, when land returned to original owners, while the sabbatical year falls every seventh year.

examples.everyday: My neighbor is on sabbatical this year, so he's finally fixing up his garage.
examples.professional: Our director is taking a sabbatical next spring, so I'll be covering her projects.
examples.analytical: The sabbatical year in Leviticus 25 joins social justice with agricultural rest, teaching that the land belongs to God.

nuance.analogy: Like a planned reset for a machine that has run too long without maintenance.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin sabbaticus, from Greek sabbatikos, from Hebrew shabbat, rest.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying suh-BAT-ih-kul is correct but sa-BAH-tical is not.
Using sabbatical for any vacation; it means a longer, planned leave.
nuance.biblical_note: Hebrew shemittah (release), often called the sabbatical year. Leviticus 25:1-7 commands that the land rest every seventh year, with no sowing or pruning. Exodus 23:10-11 gives a similar command to let the land lie fallow. Deuteronomy 15:1-2 connects the year with the release of debts.

senses.definition: The belief that observance of the sacraments is necessary for salvation, or belief in their efficacy.
The belief that the natural world is a reflection or imitation of a perfect supernatural one.
senses.example: His professor's sacramentalism led him to see God's grace in every ordinary harvest field.

core.definition: The belief that the sacraments are necessary or effective means of grace, or that material things can convey spiritual reality.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MEN, and the -ism ending is a reduced uhm. Avoid saying sak-ruh-men-TAL-iz-um, which shifts the stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it names a theological position and can be used critically or approvingly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sacramentalism mostly in academic theology, church history and denominational debates. It is not everyday talk. Protestant writers often use it to describe Catholic or Orthodox views, sometimes with a critical tone.

distinctions.note: Sacramentalism is a belief or system that gives sacraments special efficacy, while sacramentality is the quality of being sacramental.
Symbolism means that something represents a truth, while sacramentalism holds that the sign actually conveys the grace it signifies.

examples.professional: Our seminary course on church history compares Reformed and Catholic sacramentalism in one module.
examples.analytical: Critics of medieval sacramentalism argued that grace was reduced to outward rites rather than received by faith.

nuance.analogy: Sacramentalism is like believing the key itself opens the door, not only that it points to the lock.
nuance.etymology: From sacrament plus the suffix -ism.
common_mistakes: Using it for a general love of ritual, when it means a specific theological belief
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in sacramentALism

traditions.view: Orthodox Christians hold that the mysteries are real means of union with God, received in the Church, and do not see grace as only symbolic.
Catholics teach that the sacraments truly confer grace through Christ's action, so they are necessary and effective means of salvation.
Lutherans and Anglicans affirm the sacraments as real means of grace, while Reformed Christians see them as signs and seals received by faith, and Baptists treat them as memorial ordinances.

senses.definition: One who practices sacramentalism.

core.definition: A person who believes in and emphasizes the importance of the sacraments as channels of God's grace.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle syllables to quick, weak vowels. The '-ment-' and '-tal-' endings are unstressed and short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in theological writing; it can sound pointed or accusatory when used by critics of a particular view.
nuance.usage_note: The term is mainly used in theological discussion, especially among Anglicans, Lutherans, Roman Catholics, and Orthodox Christians. Americans in everyday church life would more likely say someone takes communion very seriously or emphasizes the sacraments. Some Protestant critics use the word as a label, so context matters.

distinctions.note: Sacramentarian is a term from Reformation debates for those who held a particular view of the Lord's Supper, and it can be pejorative; sacramentalist is broader and more neutral.
A ritualist emphasizes ceremonial forms in general, while a sacramentalist focuses specifically on the sacraments as means of grace.

examples.everyday: My friend, an Anglo-Catholic, calls herself a sacramentalist and never skips communion, even on a busy Sunday.
examples.professional: In his sermon series, the pastor, a self-described sacramentalist, urged the congregation to receive communion every week.
examples.analytical: Unlike the memorialist, the sacramentalist insists that grace is mediated through the material signs of baptism and the Lord's Supper.

nuance.analogy: Like a person who believes a letter carries the writer's presence, the sacramentalist believes the sacraments carry God's grace.
nuance.etymology: From sacrament, from Latin sacramentum (oath, pledge), plus the suffix -ist.
common_mistakes: Confusing sacramentalist (a person) with sacramentalism (the belief system).
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in sack-ruh-MEN-tuh-list.
nuance.biblical_note: The word sacrament is not in Scripture. The New Testament Greek word mysterion (mystery, hidden purpose) was later rendered by the Latin sacramentum in the Vulgate at Ephesians 5:32, and the sacramental practices rest on Matthew 26:26-28, which describes Jesus giving bread and wine at the Last Supper. First Corinthians 11:23-26 recounts the same institution of the Lord's Supper and Paul's instruction about remembering Christ. Romans 6:3-4 links baptism with dying and rising with Christ.

traditions.view: The Orthodox speak of seven mysteries, which they regard as means of participating in divine life, and the Divine Liturgy is central. The term sacramentalism is less used, but the mysteries are real channels of grace.

The Church recognizes seven sacraments instituted by Christ, which confer grace through the rite itself. A sacramentalist in this tradition affirms that God's grace is mediated through these visible signs.

Most Protestants recognize two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper. Lutherans and Anglicans affirm some form of real presence, the Reformed hold a spiritual presence, and Baptists and many evangelicals treat them as ordinances or memorials.

senses.definition: The property of being sacred.

core.definition: The quality of being sacred, meaning deserving deep respect, reverence, or protection from violation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the middle '-id' short. The final '-ness' is a short, unstressed syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses respect, reverence, and the value of something that should not be violated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sacredness in discussions of religion, human dignity, family, and public debates about the sanctity of life. In casual speech they more often say something is special or sacred to me. The word is common in both formal and everyday American English.

distinctions.note: Holiness refers specifically to divine purity or moral perfection, while sacredness can describe the respect due to people, places, or traditions.
Sanctity is a more formal term for inviolability, often used in debates such as the sanctity of life, while sacredness is broader and more everyday.

examples.everyday: There's a real sacredness to Sunday mornings at my dad's house, and we never schedule anything then.
examples.professional: We treat the production database with a certain sacredness, so no one changes it without a formal review.
examples.analytical: The argument rests on the sacredness of the human person, rather than on utility or social consent.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone set in the center of a village square, sacredness marks something as the center that others must respect.
nuance.etymology: From sacred plus the suffix -ness, from Latin sacer (holy).
common_mistakes: Confusing sacredness with sacrilege, which is an act that violates something sacred.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'red' sound instead of a short 'rid.'

senses.definition: Emotionally negative.
senses.example: She gets sad when he's away.

senses.definition: Feeling sorrow; sorrowful, mournful.
senses.example: She gets sad when he's away.

senses.definition: Appearing sorrowful.
senses.example: The puppy had a sad little face.

senses.definition: Causing sorrow; lamentable.
senses.example: It's a sad fact that most rapes go unreported.

senses.definition: Poor in quality, bad; shameful, deplorable; later, regrettable, poor.
senses.example: That's the saddest-looking pickup truck I've ever seen.

senses.definition: Of colors: dark, deep; later, somber, dull.
senses.example: She painted the shutters a sad green, deep and somber against the pale walls.

senses.definition: Naughty; troublesome; wicked.
senses.example: That sad little dog chewed through another pair of my shoes.

senses.definition: Unfashionable; socially inadequate or undesirable.
senses.example: I can't believe you use drugs; you're so sad!

senses.definition: Heavy; weighty; ponderous; close; hard.
senses.example: sad bread

senses.definition: Expressing contempt, ridicule or disgust; bah!
senses.example: Sad! You expect us to believe that story?

core.definition: Feeling unhappy or sorrowful, or showing that feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Pronounce it with a short a, like the a in cat, and a clear d at the end. Do not add a vowel after the d.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unhappiness, though it can be gentle when someone is comforting another person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'sad' very often in everyday speech, for example 'I'm sad you're leaving.' For a stronger feeling, people may say 'heartbroken' or 'devastated.' Calling something 'sad' can also mean pitiful or embarrassing, as in 'That's sad,' so context matters.

distinctions.note: Unhappy is a milder, more general word for not being pleased. Sad usually refers to a feeling of sorrow, often about a loss or disappointment.
Depressed can describe a serious medical condition, while sad is a normal emotion that usually passes.

examples.everyday: I'm really sad that you're moving to Denver, but I'm happy for you.
examples.professional: I'm sad to say the project was canceled, but the team learned a lot from it.
examples.analytical: The poem moves from anger to a quiet sadness, and that shift is what gives its ending weight.

nuance.analogy: Sadness is like a gray cloud over the day: it doesn't last forever, but it changes how everything looks.
nuance.etymology: From Old English sæd, meaning weary or sated, which later came to mean sorrowful.
common_mistakes: Using sad for the illness depression, which needs a more serious word.
Saying 'I am sad for you' when you mean 'I'm sorry to hear that'; Americans often prefer 'I'm sorry' in that situation.

conversation.text: I was sad to hear that Mike is moving away.
It's kind of sad that the old bookstore is closing.
The movie was so sad. I cried at the end.

senses.definition: Something that serves as a guard or protection; a defense.
senses.example: Getting a flu shot is a good safeguard against illness.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, defends or protects; defense; protection.
A safe-conduct or passport, especially in time of war.
To protect, to keep safe.
senses.example: She kept a savings to safeguard against debt and emergencies.

senses.definition: To escort safely.

core.definition: To protect something or someone from harm, loss, or danger, usually by taking planned steps.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable has a clear ar sound, as in 'card'. Do not pronounce the second syllable as 'gard' with a soft a; keep the American r.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It implies responsible protection and care.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use safeguard in business, government, and technology contexts, such as 'safeguard our data' or 'safeguard our rights.' In casual talk people more often say 'protect' or 'keep safe.' As a noun, safeguard is common in policy, and it often means a rule or measure that protects.

distinctions.note: Protect is the everyday general word. Safeguard is more formal and suggests planned, preventive measures.
Defend implies resisting an attack, while safeguard usually refers to preventing harm before it happens.

examples.everyday: We need to safeguard our passwords, so please don't write them on sticky notes.
examples.professional: We are adding two-factor authentication to safeguard customer accounts from unauthorized access.
examples.analytical: The church's creeds were designed to safeguard the apostolic faith against distortions that threatened the community's understanding of Christ.

nuance.analogy: To safeguard something is like putting a fence around a garden so that animals cannot get in and eat the plants.
nuance.etymology: Compounded from safe and guard, combining the ideas of safety and watch.
common_mistakes: Writing safegard with one g, or spelling it as two words.
Using safeguard as a verb with 'from' in the wrong place; say 'safeguard against' or 'safeguard from' only in the right context, and 'against' is more common.

safeguard.etymology: From Middle English *savegard*, from Middle French *sauvegarde*, from Old French *salve* *garde*, *sauve* *garde*, reconstructed as *safe* + *guard*.

senses.definition: The quality of being sage, wise, or able to make good decisions; the quality of being perceptive, astute or insightful.
senses.example: See Thesaurus:wisdom

core.definition: The quality of having keen judgment, insight and practical wisdom, especially in making good decisions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GAS, the second syllable, not on the first. The middle vowel is a reduced schwa, and the final -ity is pronounced tee, not tih-tee.

nuance.connotation: Positive
nuance.usage_note: This is a formal word used in essays, reviews, leadership writing or praise for an advisor. Americans rarely use it in casual speech. To compliment someone's judgment in conversation, say "you have good instincts" or "you're really wise about this."

distinctions.note: Wisdom is broad and can include moral or spiritual understanding; sagacity is narrower and focuses on shrewd, practical judgment.
Intelligence is raw mental ability; sagacity is the good judgment that uses intelligence well.

examples.everyday: Her sagacity about people is why everyone in the neighborhood asks her for advice.
examples.professional: Her sagacity in handling the vendor dispute saved us from a costly lawsuit.
examples.analytical: The historian argues that the founders' political sagacity lay less in grand theory than in their knowledge of human limits.

nuance.analogy: Sagacity is like a good compass: it doesn't show every detail of the terrain, but it reliably points you the right way.
nuance.etymology: From Latin sagacitas, from sagax, keen-scented, wise.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, which makes it sound like SAY-guh-sity.
Using it for knowledge of facts; sagacity is about judgment, not information.

sagacity.etymology: From French *sagacité*, from Latin *sagācitās* (“sagaciousness”), from *sagāx* (“of quick perception, acute, sagacious”) (whence *-acity*), from *sāgiō* (“to perceive by the senses”).

senses.definition: A rare silicate of magnesium and aluminum (with iron as a major impurity), named for its sapphirelike color.
Of, pertaining to, or resembling sapphire.

core.definition: Resembling sapphire, especially in its deep, bright blue color.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAF, and make the 'ph' an f sound. The last syllable rhymes with 'mine', and the middle 'uh' is a quick reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests beauty, richness, and a jewel-like brilliance.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in ordinary speech; they say 'sapphire blue' or simply 'blue'. You will find 'sapphirine' in poetry, nature writing, and gemology. As a noun it names a rare magnesium-aluminum silicate mineral, which is a technical use.

distinctions.note: 'Sapphire' is the gem itself, and as an adjective it is common in phrases like 'sapphire blue'; 'sapphirine' is a more literary way to say 'like a sapphire'.
'Azure' describes a bright sky-blue and is more common in poetry; 'sapphirine' suggests a deeper, more jewel-like blue.

examples.professional: The gemologist described the sample's sapphirine tint in the lab report for the buyer.
examples.analytical: Some Romantic poets used sapphirine imagery to suggest a light that is both precious and remote.

nuance.analogy: Like a gem held up to the light, a sapphirine color seems to glow from inside rather than simply reflecting light.
nuance.etymology: From sapphire, from Latin sapphirus, from Greek sappheiros, with the suffix -ine, 'of the nature of.'
common_mistakes: Using 'sapphirine' in everyday speech where 'sapphire blue' is more natural.
Confusing the adjective with the mineral noun, which is a specialized term.

senses.definition: A deep cooking vessel with a long protruding handle and sometimes a lid; used for boiling, stewing and making sauces.
To cook in a saucepan.
senses.example: I saucepan the leftover rice with a splash of broth and some frozen peas for lunch.

senses.definition: To hit with a saucepan.
senses.example: Furious, my grandmother threatened to saucepan the next burglar who tried to climb through the window.

core.definition: A deep cooking pot with one long handle and usually a lid, used for boiling, simmering, and making sauces.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SAUCE-pan, with the vowel of 'saw' rather than 'sass'. The second syllable is short and unstressed, so don't add an extra syllable at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a plain, everyday kitchen word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use saucepan for a small, deep pot with one long handle, and they say pot for a larger, deeper one with two handles. The word appears everywhere in home cooking, recipes, and kitchen stores. The verb sense is rare and mostly jokey, so use the noun in ordinary conversation.

distinctions.note: A pot is usually larger and deeper, often with two handles; a saucepan is smaller with a single long handle.
A skillet is wide and shallow with sloping sides, made for frying rather than boiling liquids.

collocations: simmer the sauce in a saucepan

examples.everyday: Can you grab the small saucepan so I can heat up some milk for the kids?
examples.professional: Our test kitchen standardized on a two-quart saucepan for every reduction sauce in the new menu.
examples.analytical: The saucepan's thin base, more than its handle, determined how unevenly the béchamel thickened over the flame.

nuance.analogy: Like a small, deep bowl that sits on a burner, with a long handle to hold it by.
nuance.etymology: From sauce plus pan; sauce comes from Latin salsa, meaning salted.
common_mistakes: Writing sauce pan as two words in the noun sense; the standard spelling is one word, saucepan.
Confusing it with a skillet, which is wide and shallow for frying.

senses.definition: The property of being scalable.
senses.example: The startup's biggest concern was the scalability of its database under heavy traffic.

core.definition: The ability of a system to handle growth in users, data or workload without losing performance or becoming too costly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'BIL', the third syllable of the noun. Do not say 'ah-bil-i-ty'; the vowels in the last syllables are reduced to 'uh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes a valued quality of systems and businesses.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scalability constantly in tech, startup and business meetings. It is usually paired with words like design, improve or test. Outside work, people rarely say it.

distinctions.note: Performance is how fast a system works now; scalability is how well it keeps working as it grows.
Capacity is the amount a system can hold; scalability is the ability to increase that amount.

examples.everyday: My phone app has no scalability at all, so it slows down when too many people log in.
examples.professional: We need to test scalability before the holiday traffic spike hits our checkout service.
examples.analytical: The theory's scalability is questionable: its methods work on small samples but break down on large populations.

nuance.analogy: Like a highway that can add lanes as traffic grows without tearing up the whole road.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun scalability with the adjective scalable.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'skay-luh-BIL-i-tee' with heavy vowels.

senses.definition: The act of something being scanned.
senses.example: Airport scanning slowed the line, so we missed our connecting flight to Denver.

core.definition: The act of examining something systematically by moving over it, often with an electronic device, to capture or find information.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the middle vowel a short 'i' as in 'sit'. The final '-ing' is a short, unstressed syllable, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a process and carries no positive or negative judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scanning in office, medical, and computing contexts, such as document scanning, security scanning, or medical scanning. In everyday speech it can also mean a quick look over something. Americans say scanner for the device, so scanning refers only to the action or process.

distinctions.note: Screening is checking people or items for a specific condition or threat, while scanning is a broader process of capturing or inspecting.
Reading means taking in the full content, while scanning means moving quickly over material to find something specific.

examples.everyday: The pharmacy's scanning system was down, so the cashier wrote down the prices by hand.
examples.professional: Our team set up automatic scanning to catch security vulnerabilities before each release.
examples.analytical: Scanning the literature produces a pattern, but it does not establish a causal explanation.

nuance.analogy: Scanning is like running a flashlight over a dark shelf until one label catches the light.
common_mistakes: Using scanning when you mean the machine, which is a scanner
Confusing scanning with screening in medical contexts

senses.definition: In a scathing manner.

core.definition: In a very harsh, cutting way that openly shows disapproval or contempt.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the final th voiced, like 'bathe'. The -ingly ending is unstressed, so say SKAY-thing-lee, not skay-THING-lee.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it signals harsh criticism or contempt, often in reviews, debates or the press.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use scathingly mostly in news reports, book reviews and political commentary, as in 'the senator scathingly criticized the bill'. In casual talk, people say 'totally trashed it' or 'tore it apart'. If someone quotes a scathing remark to you, a natural reply is 'Ouch, that's harsh'.

distinctions.note: Harshly is general and neutral, while scathingly adds a sense of biting wit and open contempt.
Bitterly stresses the speaker's resentment or grief, while scathingly stresses the cutting force of the words themselves.

examples.everyday: My sister reviewed that new burger place scathingly, saying the fries tasted like cardboard.
examples.professional: Our VP scathingly rejected the forecast in the review, calling the model's assumptions naive.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard scathingly mocked the comfortable Christianity of his day, which he saw as a polite substitute for real faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a sharp knife rather than a blunt hammer: it cuts precisely and leaves the wound visible.
nuance.etymology: From scathing, the present participle of scathe, from Old Norse skathi, harm.
common_mistakes: Stressing the -ing syllable, saying skay-THING-lee instead of SKAY-thing-lee.
Using it for mild disagreement, when it signals strong and open contempt.
Pronouncing the final th as voiceless, like 'thin', instead of voiced, like 'bathe'.

senses.definition: That scintillates with brief flashes of light; sparkling.
Brilliantly or impressively clever, exciting, amusing or witty.
senses.example: Her scintillating lecture on Augustine made even the skeptics in the back row lean forward.

core.definition: Very clever, lively, or exciting; also sparkling with brief flashes of light.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'lay', the third syllable. The first two syllables are quick and reduced, so 'sin-tuh' runs together.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises brilliance, wit, or liveliness. Used ironically it can be mildly mocking.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'scintillating' to praise a speaker, a discussion, or a performance that is unusually bright and engaging. It is often said ironically, as in 'a scintillating meeting,' meaning the opposite. It sounds rather formal in casual talk, so use it mostly in writing or in polite compliments.

distinctions.note: 'Exciting' is everyday and broad; 'scintillating' suggests brilliant wit or intelligence and is more formal.
'Sparkling' is common for light or conversation; 'scintillating' is stronger and more formal in its praise.

examples.everyday: Dinner with my aunt was scintillating, she had stories about every place she's ever lived.
examples.professional: The keynote was scintillating, and three people asked me afterward for the slides.
examples.analytical: Her scintillating critique exposes the hidden assumptions behind the entire policy debate.

nuance.analogy: A scintillating conversation is like fireworks: quick, bright bursts that keep your attention.
nuance.etymology: From the verb 'scintillate', from Latin scintillare, 'to sparkle'.
common_mistakes: Using it sincerely for something dull, which sounds sarcastic to Americans.
Putting the stress on the first syllable instead of the third.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, screens.
senses.example: The hospital hired a new screener to check visitors at the entrance each morning.

senses.definition: A question or survey used to filter potential participants based on some characteristic.
senses.example: The survey began with a screener asking whether respondents had visited a dentist this year.

senses.definition: An advance screening of a film sent to critics, awards voters, etc.
senses.example: Critics received a screener of the thriller two weeks before its theatrical release.

senses.definition: A cinema having the specified number of screens.
senses.example: The old single-screener on Main Street closed, leaving the town with no movie theater.

senses.definition: A player setting a screen for a teammate in an offensive sequence.
senses.example: The guard came off a strong screener from our center and drained a three-pointer.

senses.definition: (historical) A person employed to filter the mined coal through a metal screen to remove impurities.
senses.example: Her great-grandfather worked as a screener at the colliery, sorting coal from slate by hand.
senses.label: historical

core.definition: A short set of questions used to decide whether a person qualifies for a study, survey, job, or program.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SKREE. The final -er is a reduced, r-colored vowel, so do not say 'screen-ay'. Do not confuse it with 'screening', which has an -ing ending.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a procedural step and carries no judgment about the person answering.
nuance.usage_note: Common in American market research, clinical trial recruitment, hiring, and customer panels. Someone might say 'I didn't pass the screener' or 'Fill out the screener first.' In casual talk people more often say 'the qualifying questions'. A natural reply is 'Yes, I qualified' or 'Sorry, I didn't make the cut.'

distinctions.note: A screener is usually the questionnaire itself, while screening is the process of checking people or things against criteria.
A filter is any method or rule that removes items, while a screener is a specific set of questions used to qualify respondents.

examples.everyday: I had to fill out a screener before the clinic would book me for the sleep study.
examples.professional: Let's add a screener question about current role so we only recruit people who manage analysts.
examples.analytical: A screener calibrates the sample by excluding respondents whose characteristics would bias the estimate of the population parameter.

nuance.analogy: A bouncer checking names at the door before anyone gets into the study.
nuance.etymology: Formed from screen plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who does the action.
common_mistakes: Using 'screener' to mean the candidate who passed, as in 'I was a screener'; the set of questions is the screener, and the person passes it.
Pronouncing the final syllable as a full 'air' or 'ee' sound instead of the light American -er.

senses.definition: Any material used to seal a surface so as to prevent passage of a fluid.
senses.example: Apply a thin bead of sealant around the window frame before the spring rains start.

senses.definition: A mixture of polymers, fillers, and pigments used to fill and seal joints where moderate movement is expected.
senses.example: Use a flexible sealant to fill the expansion joints between the concrete slabs on the patio.

core.definition: A material, such as caulk or resin, applied to close gaps or joints and keep water, air or other fluids from passing through.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The long ee sound comes from seal, and the final -ant is reduced to a quick unt.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a practical trade term with associations of protection and durability.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sealant in construction, home improvement, auto repair and manufacturing. In everyday talk people often say caulk for gaps around bathtubs and windows, and sealer for coatings on wood or concrete. At a hardware store, asking for silicone sealant is a common and clear request.

distinctions.note: Caulk is a flexible material for small gaps in buildings; sealant is the broader term that includes caulk and other materials.
A sealer is usually a coating that protects a surface; a sealant fills joints and gaps to block leaks.
A gasket is a shaped piece placed between parts to seal them, while a sealant is applied as a liquid or paste.

examples.everyday: Can you pick up some silicone sealant at the hardware store? The tub is leaking again.
examples.professional: The new sealant meets the building code for moisture resistance at the window joints.
examples.analytical: In structural engineering, the performance of a sealant depends on its elasticity as much as on its adhesion to the surface.

nuance.analogy: A sealant is like a bandage for a building: it covers the crack so water cannot get in.
nuance.etymology: From seal (verb) plus -ant; seal comes from Old French seel, from Latin sigillum meaning small sign or seal.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable with the vowel of ant; it is a reduced unt sound.
Using sealant for caulk in everyday talk without thinking; Americans usually say caulk for a bathtub gap.

senses.definition: Rigid adherence to a particular sect, denomination, ideology, or party.
senses.example: They were discussing sectarianism between Shias and Sunnis.

senses.definition: A political system in which power is shared among religious sects based on a constitutional formula distributing public offices among these sects.
senses.example: In Lebanese sectarianism, one half of the members of parliament are Christians and the other half are Muslims.

core.definition: Strong, narrow loyalty to one religious, political or ideological group, often leading to hostility toward other groups.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAIR, the second syllable. The -ism ending is a reduced syllable, pronounced um, and the middle ee is a light, quick vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a harmful attitude of division and exclusion, so it is almost always used as criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sectarianism' in academic, political and religious writing, and in news about conflicts between religious or ethnic groups. In everyday talk they usually say 'tribalism' or 'partisanship' for a similar idea. Using it about a person can sound like an accusation, so explain the specific behavior.

distinctions.note: Tribalism is a broader term for loyalty to any close group, while sectarianism specifically concerns religious or doctrinal factions.
Partisanship refers to loyalty to a political party, whereas sectarianism can also describe religious or ideological groups.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of the sectarianism in our family group chat, where everyone just shouts at the other side.
examples.professional: Our policy training addresses sectarianism in the workplace, so all staff are treated fairly regardless of their beliefs.
examples.analytical: Historians argue that sectarianism in early modern Europe was driven as much by politics as by theology.

nuance.analogy: Like a fence built around one yard so tightly that neighbors on the other side cannot even see your garden.
nuance.etymology: From 'sectarian' with the suffix -ism, meaning a doctrine or attitude, from Latin secta.
common_mistakes: Using sectarianism as a synonym for religion; it refers to narrow division, not faith itself.
Writing sectarian (adjective) when you need the noun form sectarianism.

senses.definition: In a secure manner; without fear or apprehension; without danger.
senses.example: Check all personal items are securely stowed in the overhead lockers.

core.definition: In a safe, stable way that is protected from danger, loss, or fear.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, kyoor. The r is pronounced clearly, and the first vowel is a weak schwa, not 'see'.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it signals safety, stability, and confidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use securely to describe fastening, locking, or storing things, as in 'Make sure the door is securely locked.' It can also describe feelings of safety, but that use is more formal. In everyday talk, people often say 'safely' or 'tight' instead when fastening something.

distinctions.note: Safely focuses on avoiding harm; securely focuses on being firmly fixed or protected against loss or intrusion.
Firmly describes pressure or strength; securely describes stable protection or fastening.

examples.everyday: Before we leave for the trip, make sure the luggage is securely strapped to the roof of the car.
examples.professional: Please make sure all server racks are securely mounted before the maintenance window opens.
examples.analytical: The psalmist describes the righteous as dwelling securely, a condition grounded in trust rather than in material safety.

nuance.analogy: Securely is like a knot pulled tight: it holds firm because each part is fixed in place.
nuance.etymology: From secure (from Latin securus, free from care) plus the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, which makes the word sound off to Americans.
Using securely for simple safety of a person; 'safely' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Hebrew Bible, the idea of dwelling securely is often expressed by the root betach (bitachon), meaning trust, confidence, or secure reliance on God. Proverbs 1:33 says that whoever listens to wisdom will dwell securely and be free from dread of evil. Jeremiah 23:6 promises that Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell securely under the righteous Branch of David.

senses.definition: Relating to the Greek-Macedonian dynasty which ruled (312–63 BCE) an empire created by Seleucus out of the eastern conquests of Alexander the Great.
A member of this dynasty.
senses.example: The historian argued that the Seleucid king had lost control of the eastern provinces by 200 BCE.

core.definition: Relating to the Greek dynasty that ruled much of Alexander's eastern empire from 312 to 63 BCE.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'LOO', the second syllable. The 'eu' is pronounced like 'oo', so don't say 'SEL-yoo-sid'. The final '-id' is short.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a historical label. Readers of Jewish history may associate it with persecution under Antiochus IV.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Seleucid' mainly in history, classics, and religious studies, usually as an adjective ('Seleucid coins', 'Seleucid rule') and sometimes as a noun for a member of the dynasty. It almost never appears in everyday talk. When you mention it in a class or a church study, stress the middle syllable 'LOO'.
word_family: Seleucus (proper noun, founder of the dynasty)

distinctions.note: 'Ptolemaic' refers to the rival Greek dynasty in Egypt; 'Seleucid' refers to the dynasty based in Syria and the east.
'Hellenistic' is a broad period label for Greek-influenced culture after Alexander; 'Seleucid' names one dynasty within that period.
'Macedonian' names a region of origin; 'Seleucid' names a specific ruling family.

examples.everyday: My history class spent the whole week on the Seleucid kings who came after Alexander.
examples.professional: Our museum's new exhibit features Seleucid coins from the mint at Antioch.
examples.analytical: Seleucid policy toward Judea shaped the crisis described in 1 Maccabees, so the empire's politics matter for reading that text.

nuance.analogy: Like the Tudors in English history: one royal family that gave its name to a whole era.
nuance.etymology: From Seleucus I Nicator, the Macedonian general who founded the dynasty.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'SEL-yoo-sid'; the stress is on 'LOO'.
Confusing it with 'Ptolemaic', the rival Egyptian dynasty.
nuance.biblical_note: The Seleucid kings ruled Syria and, for a period, Judea before the Maccabean revolt. The term is a modern name taken from the founder Seleucus, so no Hebrew or Greek word stands behind it, and the biblical texts speak of the king of Syria or the kings of the north. First Maccabees 1:10-64 and 2 Maccabees 6:1-11 describe the persecution under Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Daniel 11:21-35 describes conflicts between the kings of the north and the king of the south, which many readers connect with the Seleucid and Ptolemaic rulers.

seleucid.etymology: From Latin *Seleucides*, from Ancient Greek *Σελευκίδης*, named after Seleucus I Nicator.

related: Seleucus (proper noun, founder of the dynasty)

senses.definition: Someone who sells; a vendor; a clerk.
senses.example: Alisha was a seller of fine books.

senses.definition: Something which sells.
senses.example: Two of the books Alisha authored had become big sellers.

core.definition: A person or company that sells something, such as a home, car or product, to a buyer.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, SEL. The second syllable is a reduced American 'er,' like 'teller,' not a long 'ee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a role in a transaction, without praise or blame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'seller' in real estate, online marketplaces and everyday shopping. For a clerk in a store, people usually say 'salesperson' or 'the person at the counter.' In real estate, 'seller' is the person selling a house, and 'buyer' is the other party. The word is common and natural in both business and casual talk.

distinctions.note: Vendor is a more formal or business term for a supplier or someone who sells to others, often in procurement.
Salesperson refers to an employee who sells products, while seller can be any individual or business selling something.
Merchant is a more traditional or formal word for someone who buys and sells goods for profit.

examples.everyday: The seller said I could come by Saturday to pick up the couch.
examples.professional: The third-party seller on our marketplace needs a faster return policy for electronics.
examples.analytical: Economists model the seller's decision as a trade-off between a higher price and a faster sale.

nuance.analogy: Like the person behind the counter who holds the product until someone agrees to pay for it.
nuance.etymology: From sell + -er.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a long 'ee' sound like 'SEE-ler'; the vowel is short.
Using 'seller' for a store clerk in everyday talk; 'salesperson' is more natural.

seller.etymology: From Middle English *seller*, *sellere*, (also *siller*, *sullar*, *sullere*), from Old English **sellere*, **syllere*, equivalent to *sell* + *-er* (sense 1) and *sell* + *-er* (sense 2).

senses.definition: In a sensational manner.
To a sensational extent; amazingly.
senses.example: The rookie pitcher performed sensationally, striking out fourteen batters in his first start.

core.definition: In a dramatic or shocking manner; also, extremely or impressively, as in informal praise.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'SAY', and the final syllable '-ly' is a clear 'lee' with a long e. The middle syllables are reduced to a schwa.

nuance.connotation: Mixed. In news reporting it is negative, but in casual praise it can be positive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sensationally mostly in the sense of dramatically or shockingly, as in 'the story was sensationally reported'. In casual speech, people sometimes say something was sensationally good, but this is less common than 'amazingly' or 'incredibly'. Choose the sense from context.

distinctions.note: Amazingly is a neutral intensifier, while sensationally often implies a dramatic or shocking quality.
Dramatically describes a change or action with force; sensationally often describes a shocking presentation or result.

examples.everyday: The sandwich place down the street is sensationally good, so get there before lunch rush.
examples.professional: The beta launch went sensationally well, with adoption climbing far faster than our forecast.
examples.analytical: The newspaper sensationally portrayed the scandal, reducing a complex institutional failure to a single villain.

nuance.analogy: Sensationally is like a fireworks show: it grabs attention with loud, dramatic effects.
nuance.etymology: From sensational plus -ly, 'in a manner of'.
common_mistakes: Using sensationally with a neutral meaning in news contexts, where it usually implies exaggeration.
Confusing sensationally with sensibly, which means reasonably or wisely.

senses.definition: A love song that is sung directly to one's love interest, especially one performed below the window of a loved one in the evening.
senses.example: He stood beneath her window with a guitar, ready to sing a serenade.

senses.definition: An instrumental composition in several movements.
senses.example: “Eine kleine Nachtmusik” is a well-known serenade written by Mozart.

senses.definition: To sing or play a serenade for (someone).
senses.example: On their anniversary, the band serenaded the couple with old love songs at dinner.

senses.definition: To woo someone.
senses.example: He spent the whole spring trying to serenade her with flowers, poems, and long walks.

core.definition: A love song sung or played for someone, often at night, traditionally under the window of the person being courted.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the last syllable, -NAYD, and keep the first syllable light, not 'SAIR-uh-nade'. The word is the same stress whether used as a noun or a verb.

nuance.connotation: Positive and romantic. It can also be used playfully, such as a funny song at a party.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use serenade for romantic songs, especially in movies, weddings and proposals, and sometimes as a joke. People talk about serenading a partner at Valentine's Day or a mariachi band serenading a table. The verb is common and mostly playful or romantic; the noun is somewhat more literary.

distinctions.note: A ballad is a story-song or sentimental song, not necessarily addressed to a loved one, while a serenade is sung directly to a beloved.
A love song can be recorded or heard anywhere, while a serenade is a live performance aimed at one person, often outdoors at night.

examples.everyday: My roommate serenaded his girlfriend under her window last night, and the whole block was awake.
examples.professional: The team wrote a funny serenade for the CEO's retirement party, and everyone sang along.
examples.analytical: Troubadour poetry often framed the serenade as a bond between desire and restraint, with the singer exposed to the night while the beloved stays unseen.

nuance.analogy: A serenade is like a personal radio broadcast: one singer, one listener, and the whole evening set up for a single audience.
nuance.etymology: From Italian serenata, an evening song, from sereno, clear or calm, from Latin serenus.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, saying 'SAIR-uh-nade' instead of sair-uh-NAYD.
Using serenade for any sad or quiet song, when it means a song sung directly to someone.

serenade.etymology: French *sérénade*, from Italian *serenata*, from the past participle of *serenare*, from Latin *serenare*, from *serenus* (“calm”), of uncertain origin.

senses.definition: A partially free peasant of a low hereditary class, attached like a slave to the land owned by a feudal lord and required to perform labor, enjoying minimal legal or customary rights.
senses.example: In medieval England, a serf worked the lord's fields and could not leave the manor freely.

senses.definition: A similar agricultural laborer in 18th and 19th century Europe.
senses.example: Her great-grandfather worked as a serf on a Polish estate in the 1830s.

senses.definition: A worker unit.
senses.example: Each node in the cluster runs a serf agent that reports health to the central server.

core.definition: A peasant in medieval Europe who was legally tied to a lord's land, had to work for him, and had few rights to leave or own property.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the American r-colored sound, so serf sounds exactly like surf. Do not pronounce a separate e sound, as in 'sair-f'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes oppression, lack of freedom, and forced labor.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use serf mainly in history classes and discussions of feudalism or Russian history. Calling modern workers serfs is a strong political or emotional statement and can sound insulting or exaggerated. Use it when you are talking about the historical institution.

distinctions.note: A slave is owned as property, while a serf is bound to the land and owed labor but is not bought and sold like an object.
A peasant is any farmer of low status, while a serf is a peasant with a specific legal obligation to a lord.

examples.everyday: My history teacher said the serfs in Russia usually couldn't leave their villages without permission.
examples.professional: Calling our overworked contractors serfs in front of the board would be a serious mistake, even as a joke.
examples.analytical: Marx treated the serf as a figure whose labor was extracted through legal obligation rather than through wages in a market.

nuance.analogy: A serf is like a worker whose job is tied to a house he cannot leave, so the land holds him as much as any contract does.
nuance.etymology: From Latin servus, slave or servant, through Old French serf.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with an extra vowel, as 'sair-f', instead of the single r-colored vowel that sounds like surf.
Confusing serf with slave, which is a different legal status.

serf.etymology: From Middle English *serf*, from Old French *serf*, from Latin *servus* (“slave, serf, servant”).

senses.definition: The promotional or advertisement term used to describe the final episode of a television program, usually a situation comedy or a drama.
senses.example: Critics praised the series finale of the sitcom, which wrapped up every character's storyline.

core.definition: The last episode of a television show, meant to conclude its whole story and end the series for good.

pronunciation.tip: In a two-word compound noun, the first word gets the strongest stress, so 'SEER-eez' is stressed and 'fuh-NAL-ee' is weaker. Keep 'finale' as three syllables, with the stress on 'NAL'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to emotional. People often discuss it with excitement, disappointment, or nostalgia depending on how the ending was received.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'series finale' for the final episode of a show that will not return, and 'season finale' for the last episode of a season that may be followed by more. Fans often talk about series finales with strong opinions, so 'Did you watch the series finale?' is a very natural small-talk question.
